papers.title: TAC2: Timestamped Audio Captioning as composable functions
papers.abstract: Real-world audio applications require precise, queryable representations grounded in physical time. Yet modern Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) increasingly favor conversational generation, producing free-form descriptions that conflate acoustic perception with higher-level reasoning and lack precise temporal grounding. We introduce TAC2, a foundation model that casts timestamped audio captioning as composable functions to construct granular, speaker-attributed acoustic timelines directly from in-the-wild audio. To avoid prohibitively expensive manual annotation, we programmatically fuse complementary predictions from specialized weak teachers through time-registered IoU matching. We model the resulting multi-granularity schema of timestamped events, speaker turns, and fine-grained speech attributes using an Instruction-Input-Output (IIO) completion format, in which each task is a function of the audio, an instruction, and an optional input. A single call decodes the full description autonomously, while composing calls lets earlier outputs or external priors, such as a reference transcript, condition later ones. We further extend TAC2 with expressive speech attributes to obtain TAC2-S, using parameter-efficient specialists to elicit latent paralinguistic capabilities from the pre-trained backbone and distill them into a unified model. We validate the resulting representation in two complementary settings. Paired with frozen text-only LLMs, it yields strong spoken audio understanding across diverse reasoning backends, demonstrating the utility of decoupling fine-grained acoustic perception from downstream reasoning. Used as paired supervision for text-to-audio generation, it supports semantically and temporally grounded reconstruction, together with explicit zero-shot control over event timing, speaker attributes, and word-level emphasis.

papers.title: Audio-R1: Audio Reasoning through Reinforcement Learning on Self-Supervised Tasks
papers.abstract: Reasoning is increasingly important for large audio-language models (LALMs), yet remains relatively underexplored compared with text-only and vision-language models. We introduce Audio-R1, a reinforcement learning (RL) post-training framework that revisits audio self-supervised learning as a source of verifiable rewards for improving audio understanding and reasoning task performance. Audio-R1 uses answers automatically determined during the construction of self-supervised tasks to verify model responses and compute rewards. Experiments across multiple LALMs and diverse audio benchmarks show consistent performance gains, while ablations demonstrate the benefits of each self-supervised task and additional gains from joint training. While both supervised fine-tuning and Audio-R1 improve self-supervised task accuracy, Audio-R1 further improves performance on downstream tasks distinct from the training tasks. These results highlight the potential of RL post-training with self-supervised audio tasks to improve downstream performance and reasoning-trace quality.

papers.title: Does Notation Matter? MusicXML Tokenisation for Symbolic Music Generation and Understanding
papers.abstract: Symbolic music representations encode musical content at varying levels of completeness, from performance-oriented formats such as MIDI to fully notated scores such as MusicXML. Yet the impact of this representational richness on deep learning models remains poorly understood. While tokenisation has been extensively studied for MIDI, score-based formats have received considerably less attention, and MusicXML in particular remains largely unexplored despite being the de-facto standard for score interchange. In this paper, we introduce the first general-purpose tokenisation framework for MusicXML, and conduct a systematic empirical study to determine whether notational richness confers a measurable advantage for deep learning on symbolic music. We train 26 autoregressive and masked language models, comparing MusicXML tokenisation against MIDI and ABC-based representations, probing the effect of different tokenisation strategies within MusicXML, and testing whether music-grammar-aware tokenisation outperforms treating scores as plain text. We evaluate music understanding tasks using linear probing across composer classification, difficulty estimation, and accompaniment suggestion, and generative tasks using objective statistical metrics and a human pairwise preference study. Our results show that MusicXML-tokenised models outperform MIDI and text-based counterparts on understanding and generative tasks.

papers.title: S3-S2ST: Semantically Supervised Streaming Speech-to-Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Streaming speech-to-speech translation requires timely decisions about when partial input is sufficient for accurate translation. We present S3-S2ST, a model that learns to translate and speak from semantically aligned streaming supervision. By converting utterance-level speech pairs into incremental training examples, we teach a learned policy when to commit translations. Its adjustable threshold controls the quality--latency tradeoff on a fixed 640\,ms input grid. S3-S2ST delivers competitive English--Chinese translation on FLEURS and leads the evaluated streaming systems in translation quality on the internal 9-pair test set. On RealSI, adapting the threshold to buffered speech further improves quality over a low fixed threshold with little change in first-audio latency. We plan to release the model and code.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech translation, speech-to-speech

papers.title: In-Context Adapter Generation for Compositional Generalization in Large Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) have achieved strong performance on standard speech and audio understanding tasks, yet their ability to systematically generalize to novel task compositions remains underexplored. Taking a meta-learning view, we extend Text-to-LoRA (T2L) to LALMs, generating instruction-conditioned LoRA adapters with a Transformer hypernetwork rather than learning a single fixed adapter shared across instructions. To exploit fine-grained task information, we introduce in-context adapter generation (ICAG), a token-level hypernetwork architecture; we call the resulting method T2L-ICAG. We evaluate this approach on two representative LALMs using SIFT-50M for supervised fine-tuning and construct a controlled compositional evaluation suite covering five task classes. Across two LALM backbones, T2L-ICAG consistently improves over static LoRA and also the global embedding-based T2L baseline. Coverage and capacity analyses further show that these gains are larger on structurally out-of-domain tasks and cannot be explained by parameter count alone. These results suggest that generating task-specific adapters from instructions is a promising direction for improving compositional generalization of LALMs.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio language model
Audio Understanding & Reasoning: audio understanding

papers.title: AudioRSI: Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has made Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) better reasoners, but the reward that drives it still comes from outside the model: a final-answer check, a hand-crafted process score, or an external LLM judge that stays fixed while the policy improves. We show that an Audio LLM can supply this reward itself, and can do so recursively: each improved model becomes the critic that trains its successor, so the training signal improves along with the model. We introduce AudioRSI (Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners), a reinforcement learning framework in which a single model plays two roles: as an actor it generates reasoning paths, and as a critic it compares them pairwise, turning its own judgments into a process-level reward. The critic is periodically replaced by the current policy, which closes the recursive loop. Because the critic hears the same recording as the actor, it can reject reasoning that cites acoustic evidence the audio does not contain, rather than reward reasoning that merely sounds plausible. The recursion is what sustains progress: under a frozen external judge, out-of-distribution accuracy plateaus during training, while a critic refreshed from the improving policy keeps it rising. Across four out-of-distribution benchmarks, all disjoint from the AVQA training distribution, AudioRSI outperforms strong baselines including Audio Flamingo 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on MMAU test-mini, ranks first on MMSU, achieves a clear lead on the challenging Multi-Audio split of MMAU-Pro, and leads the 7B open-source tier on MMAR among methods without external reward models. With no reward specifying how to reason, AudioRSI also develops structured reasoning behaviors (logical reasoning, perception-aware analysis, and reduced hallucination), corroborated by an external LLM-as-Judge evaluation and a keyword-based behavior analysis.

papers.title: StreamSE: Neural Audio Codec-based Streaming Speech Enhancement for On-device Inference
papers.abstract: Recent generative speech enhancement (SE) models achieve high perceptual quality, but their non-causal processing and expensive computation make them difficult to use for streaming, on-device inference. We propose StreamSE, a 20M-parameter streaming SE model that operates in the latent space of a frozen pretrained neural audio codec. At each frame, StreamSE directly regresses a clean continuous latent from the noisy continuous latent while conditioning on its own predictions from previous frames. Enhancement therefore requires a single forward pass per frame and no iterative sampling or look-ahead. We further truncate the codec's residual vector quantizer (RVQ) to its coarse levels, halving the number of tokens per frame while improving robustness to reverberation. StreamSE is the only streaming generative model in our comparison, yet it matches or exceeds the perceptual quality of the offline generative baselines. Furthermore, the complete StreamSE pipeline runs in real time on a single smartphone CPU core. Our results show that continuous latent regression provides a practical route to generative SE under fully causal, on-device streaming constraints.
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: neural audio codec

papers.title: Developing a Speech Language Model for Basque
papers.abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech language model

papers.title: From Speech Tokens to Stolen Voices: Attacker-Chosen-Text Speaker Impersonation via Representation Inversion
papers.abstract: Speech interaction systems have gradually evolved from traditional cascaded systems that use text as intermediate information to end-to-end speech language models that directly process speech representations. In some applications, the speech frontend runs on the user's device and sends speech representations to a remote server for inference, while the original audio remains local. However, these representations may still contain speaker identity information. If an attacker obtains them, it may use this information to imitate the user's voice, threatening their voice privacy. To investigate this risk, we propose \stia, a Speech Token Inversion Attack that generates speech with attacker-specified text in a victim's voice using a single short leaked representation, without access to the original audio or its transcript. Specifically, \stia converts discrete, continuous, or mixed speech representations into conditioning sequences and trains a conditional flow-matching speech generation model using pairs of different utterances from the same speaker in public speech datasets. The model combines speaker characteristics contained in the leaked representation with the specified text to generate speech in the victim's voice. Experiments show that, with a Moshi representation leak corresponding to 3 seconds of speech, \stia achieves an average CAM++ speaker cosine similarity of 0.78 and a target-text word error rate of 3.80\%. These results show that speech frontend representations reveal reusable speaker identity information and highlight the need to consider privacy risks when designing speech frontend representation methods.

Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech generation

papers.title: AI-Based Voice to Music Generation System
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and generative models has created new opportunities for automating creative processes, particularly in music composition and audio production. Traditional music creation often requires musical knowledge, instrument-playing skills, professional audio-editing tools, and considerable time. These requirements can make music production challenging for beginners and individuals without formal musical training. To address these challenges, this research proposes an AI-Based Voice-to-Music Generation System that enables users to create musical compositions through natural voice commands. The proposed system aims to integrate speech recognition, natural language processing, audio signal processing, and AI-based music generation into a unified framework. Users can provide voice commands through a microphone or upload audio recordings describing their musical preferences. The system processes the input using speech recognition techniques to convert speech into text. Natural Language Processing is then applied to identify relevant musical characteristics, including genre, mood, tempo, and instrument preferences. Based on the extracted information, an appropriate generative music model produces a musical composition corresponding to the user's instructions. The generated audio is subsequently processed and made available for playback, saving, and downloading through an interactive user interface. The effectiveness of the proposed system will be investigated through experiments evaluating speech recognition accuracy, musical command interpretation, music generation quality, processing time, and user satisfaction. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Voice-to-Music Generation, Natural Language Processing, Speech Recognition, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Generative Music Models, Audio Signal Processing, Music Composition.
papers.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management

papers.title: Spatial Audio Generation and Editing with Executable Plans and Self-Distilling Transfusion
papers.abstract: Spatial audio authoring coordinates source decisions with soundfield synthesis. For editing, plans specify what to change and retain, while reference audio supplies further acoustic detail. We present AMBIT, a unified framework for native First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) generation and editing with three connected contributions. First, a shared Transfusion backbone couples autoregressive planning with rectified-flow rendering through executable ScenePlans that specify source content, activity, and 3D trajectories. For editing, the plan describes the full target scene, including retained sources; contrastive features ground the requested change, while full reference latents supply residual acoustic detail for preservation. Second, an FOA-aware continuous VAE combines shared-decoder omnidirectional recovery, asymmetric grouped KL, and spatial covariance matching to preserve content and inter-channel structure. Third, joint Transfusion on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) refines planning on student-generated prefixes and rendering at sampling states reached under student plans, with target-conditioned teachers supervising both modes of the shared student. Evaluations across speech, music, and sound show improved generation content and spatial quality, acoustic fidelity during instruction-guided editing, and unedited-source preservation over the compared baselines. Project page: https://wjm-george.github.io/AMBIT/
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: audio generation

papers.title: SimPOTrans: Self-Adaptation for Offline-to-Simultaneous Speech Translation via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Simultaneous speech translation (SimulST) aims to translate ongoing speech with low latency while preserving translation quality. Recent studies have adopted large language models (LLMs) for SimulST and formulated it as a multi-turn dialogue task for efficient generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, existing dialogue-style SimulST approaches typically rely on specialized training schemes to acquire simultaneous translation behavior, either using synthesized read/write trajectories, which may provide suboptimal training signals, or jointly optimizing translation quality and latency, whose competing objectives may cause optimization instability. In this paper, we introduce SimPOTrans, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that enables offline speech translation models to self-adapt to dialogue-style SimulST. Through a simple two-stage RL post-training pipeline, SimPOTrans rewards an offline model for exhibiting translation behaviors beneficial to simultaneous scenarios when given partial speech inputs, thereby enabling offline-to-simultaneous self-adaptation without synthesized read/write trajectories or explicit latency optimization. At inference time, SimPOTrans requires no external decision policy and enables flexible quality--latency control by simply adjusting the chunk size of speech input. Experiments on the ACL 60/60 and MCIF benchmarks across three language directions (En$\rightarrow$De, En$\rightarrow$Zh, and En$\rightarrow$Ja) demonstrate that SimPOTrans outperforms several strong baselines, achieving a superior quality--latency trade-off.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech translation

papers.title: ImageTTS: Repurposing Pretrained Image Diffusion Transformers for Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Pretrained image-generation models have been successfully repurposed for various downstream visual tasks. Whether their learned representations and generative priors can transfer beyond vision to other modalities remains largely unresolved, particularly for speech synthesis, which requires linguistic fidelity and preservation of speaker identity from a short reference. We present ImageTTS, which repurposes FLUX.2 for speech synthesis by encoding pseudo-RGB log-mel spectrograms with its frozen image VAE and adapting only its pretrained Diffusion Transformer (DiT) using conditional latent flow matching. This formulation disentangles two forms of vision-to-speech transfer: representation transfer through the image VAE and generative-prior transfer through DiT initialization. The frozen image VAE largely preserves intelligibility and speaker identity with 0.99 STOI and 0.95 speaker similarity, while image-pretrained DiT initialization accelerates convergence and improves linguistic accuracy, reducing WER from 4.2\% to 2.7\% at 100k matched updates relative to random initialization. The same framework supports both zero-shot and instruction-guided TTS and, when scaled to 100K hours of speech data, achieves 1.12\% WER on Seed-TTS test-en and a Style-ACC of 0.66 on CapSpeech, outperforming speech-native baselines trained on comparable data across both tasks. These results suggest that pretrained image models can transfer beyond architectural reuse, supplying useful latent representations and generative priors for intelligible and controllable speech synthesis.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech synthesis

papers.title: Understanding Everyday Communication Patterns, Stress, and Productivity in Hybrid Work through Egocentric Wearable Audio Sensing
papers.abstract: The hybrid work trend in the post-COVID period has transformed how people communicate while at work. However, there is a lack of quantitative understanding of how home and office environments shape communicative behavior and affective well-being. To study this, as a part of a larger study of the role of work environment on stress, we designed an egocentric wearable audio sensing system that captured interpersonal communication across both working locations. The system extracts real-time acoustic features on a wearable audio sensor and performs offline foreground speaker diarization to derive speaking load and activeness features. To improve diarization performance under low-dimensional feature constraints, we apply a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework that transfers knowledge from large-scale speech foundation models into a compact ResNet-based model, achieving consistent improvements in diarization performance over the baseline across three public egocentric speech datasets. In a four-month longitudinal deployment with 16 participants, our system revealed location-dependent differences in work communication patterns. Moreover, the mixed linear model analyses showed that office-based speaking load was significantly associated with higher self-reported stress and lower self-reported productivity, while speaking activeness during home-based work amplified both productivity and affective load in this cohort.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech foundation model

papers.title: Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence
papers.abstract: For audio-language models, an answer change after a local sound-event edit can reflect a response to the event's class, sensitivity to waveform rewriting, or both. We compare matched same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event. Both use the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, while the same-class replacement preserves the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, different-class replacements produce 49.7 to 60.9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements. Same-class accuracy remains within 5.2 percentage points of original accuracy. Among trials with correct original and same-class answers, soundscape-weighted selective accuracy for the inserted class is 73.7 to 81.9%, averaging eligible trials within each soundscape and then weighting eligible soundscapes equally. This protocol tests how model answers respond to local changes in event class.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio-language model

papers.title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
papers.abstract: Expanding multilingual ASR systems to new languages is challenging when adaptation must preserve previously supported languages without replaying source-language training data. We study this problem in connector-based Speech LLMs, where a trainable connector maps speech representations into a frozen large language model. We evaluate target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting the connector while preserving source-language performance. In single-target expansion, target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging learn new languages but cause severe source-language forgetting, while SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the best source-preserving trade-off. In multi-target expansion, update merging provides stable source retention, whereas recursive expansion can improve target adaptation under favorable orders but is highly order-sensitive. These results show that multilingual ASR expansion requires balancing target acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech llm

papers.title: LeanTTS: Efficient Full-Stack Bilingual TTS for Zero-Shot Cloning and Voice Customization
papers.abstract: While recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis have substantially improved speech quality and modeling flexibility, the development of lightweight and computationally efficient systems remains comparatively underexplored. We present LeanTTS, a bilingual complete synthesis stack that supports two complementary regimes: reference-prompt zero-shot cloning for unseen speakers and token-conditioned customization for recurring voices. LeanTTS combines a compact Mandarin polyphone front end, a structurally compressed flow-matching acoustic model, and a lightweight Vocos decoder with four-step MeanFlow generation. The resulting system contains 18.9M learned parameters, 86.12% fewer than the 136.2M-parameter ZipVoice-Vocos pipeline. On Seed-TTS-Eval, its zero-shot mode obtains 2.02 CER/62.3 SIM on Mandarin and 2.32 WER/48.3 SIM on English, exposing the quality-size trade-off under aggressive compression. With token-conditioned customized voices, the same system reaches 1.57 CER/77.2 SIM on Mandarin and 1.93 WER/76.6 SIM on English, with UTMOS scores of 3.03 and 4.33, respectively. It further achieves mean/P90 CPU RTFs of 0.049/0.061, establishing a sub-20M operating point for bilingual personalization and real-time CPU deployment. Audio demos are available at https://github.com/notlu/leantts.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: text-to-speech

papers.title: ASR-Protected Fusion and Reference-Anchored Policy Optimization for Joint ASR and Word-Level Speech Anti-Spoofing
papers.abstract: Existing anti-spoofing systems report either an utterance-level score or a time-based spoof interval: the former cannot show which words are spoofed, while the latter does not directly match the transcript and must be post-aligned with words, so alignment errors can lead to wrong word-level labels. Standard ASR model outputs only text; spoof information in the audio is lost after recognition and is not passed with the transcript. Yet changing only a few words can change the meaning of a sentence, leaving downstream systems to use incorrect text without knowing which words are spoofed. We therefore treat partial anti-spoofing as tagged ASR: the model transcribes speech and marks spoofed words at the same time, directly linking spoof labels to output words. We adopt the audio LLM and use ASR-Protected Subspace Gated Fusion (APSGF) to fuse spoof cues with ASR features. Spoof cues are added only outside an ASR-protected subspace, so they do not disturb recognition features. After cross-entropy training, we fine-tune the model with Reference-Anchored Policy Optimization (RAPO). Since the SFT policy is already concentrated, multiple samples from the same input tend to receive similar rewards, resulting in weak group-wise advantages. RAPO instead generates a single sample with low sampling randomness and anchors its advantage to the reward of a reference model. This allows the model to reinforce responses that outperform the reference while suppressing those that underperform it. Experiments on five datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in jointly detecting spoofed words and preserving ASR accuracy. The code is publicly available.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio llm

papers.title: Probing the phon* representations of the Mimi codebooks
papers.abstract: Neural audio codecs are increasingly used to encode speech for integration with large language models. This paper investigates the phonetic representations in the first codebook (CB0) of the Mimi codec. ABX style evaluation is poorly suited to Mimi fixed 80 ms tokenization window, which often spans multiple phonemes; we instead use forced alignment, entropy analysis, and Phone-Normalized Mutual Information (PNMI). Using TIMIT speech (58/55 speakers, SA1/SA2), individual tokens are strongly associated with specific phonemes (PNMI = 0.84, above random), yet phonemes are realized by multiple competing tokens rather than a one-to-one mapping.
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: neural audio codec

papers.title: Using an Automatic Speech Recognition Multi-Modal System in Order Selection in a Cold Storage Facility
papers.abstract: This field study evaluated a wireless, wearable Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) multi-modal system—consisting of an Android™ device, headset with a microphone, and ring scanner—for product selection in a cold storage facility. Conditions in these facilities are harsh, with temperatures ranging from −25 to −29 C, noise levels of 70–95 dBA from compressors, evaporator fans, and blast freezers, and icy floor surfaces. The ASR multi-modal system replaced radio frequency handheld scanners that were previously used for order selection. The implementation was instrumental in increased order-selection efficiency by about 30%, improved work quality, and enhanced ergonomics. All order selectors reported satisfaction with the ASR multi-modal system.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: automatic speech recognition

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Elder-Scam Defense: A Review of Detection Methods for Human- and AI-Generated Fraud and a Layered Protection Framework
papers.abstract: Scams targeting older adults increasingly combine social engineering with generative technology such as voice cloning, video deepfakes and text produced by large language models (LLMs). Adults aged 60 and over reported losses of USD 7.7 billion to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center in 2025, 59% more than in 2024. This review, supported by a documented search of four databases (2019–2026), examines how such scams are structured, why older adults are susceptible, and how artificial intelligence (AI) can detect or mitigate them. Of 992 screened records, 60 studies met the eligibility criteria, and three more were identified through citation chasing. Most evaluations with older users measured knowledge, confidence or intentions after an educational intervention; where detection performance or real-world exposure was measured, results were mixed and often null. None of the included studies evaluated an AI-based scam-detection system with older users in a field setting, and the only study testing audio-deepfake detectors on older speakers found that detectors trained on standard benchmarks roughly doubled their error rate. We propose a six-layer conceptual framework, not yet validated, for engineering elder-scam protection as a socio-technical system, and identify age-diverse evaluation, field trials of real-time assistance, privacy preservation and trust calibration as the principal open challenges.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: voice cloning

NVIDIA developed this [Speech-Augmented Language Model (SALM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.09424) for multilingual transcription, speech translation, contextual transcription, speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, timestamp prediction, language identification, and audio question answering. hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model with a Transformer audio encoder **Network Architecture:** Nemotron 3.5 Lightning hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE with Transformer ASR encoder and Sortformer speaker encoder **Design:** Audio perception module consisting of transformer ASR encoder and [Nemotron-3-Diarization](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization) speaker encoder, a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) timestamp alignment head, and [NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16) language backbone. The perception configuration uses a 1,280-dimensional identity connector followed by a learned projection to 2,688 dimensions. Audio features are combined with the text prompt for text generation. The model enables joint multi-token prediction (MTP), with two trained next-token prediction depths using a repeated layer and retaining the existing head. Reusing the repeated layer during inference supports up to eight speculative tokens. A dedicated [DFlash2](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2) draft model, a block-diffusion drafter based on DFlash, is also provided as an option for speculative decoding. **Base model:** [`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16`](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16); 600M parameter pretrained ASR transformer; and approximately 99M parameter Nemotron-3-Diarization speaker encoder. **Parameter count:** The language backbone has approximately 3.5B active parameters. Together with the approximately 800M-parameter joint audio encoder, the model has approximately 4.3B active parameters. **Precision:** Weights are released in bfloat16 (BF16), with FP8 and NVFP4 quantized variants. ## Language Support Matrix - ✓ Supported - — Not specified ASR means automatic speech recognition; code-switching means using more than one language within a recording. Audio is paired with text instructions and targets: transcripts, translations, speaker-attributed transcripts, captions, answers, and labels; a small share of the data is text-only. The content comprises public and third-party speech corpora (read speech, conversations, meetings, broadcasts, and earnings calls), web-derived speech, sound, and music, pseudo-labeled transcripts and translations, constructed multi-speaker mixtures, and synthetic data such as synthetic PII text and speech. The data covers the 40 supported languages, with the largest share in English, as well as code-switched speech. #### Training Data Size Details **Total examples, audio hours, text tokens, unique dataset count, partition percentages, and collection periods:** - Total multimodal tokens (non-unique): 479 billion - Audio share of multimodal input positions: approx. 60% - Audio tokens (non-unique): 286 billion - Text tokens (non-unique, including responses to audio examples): 193 billion - Audio examples (unique indexed records, estimated): 372,206,279 - Audio examples (non-unique, estimated): 1,780,012,724 - Audio hours (unique indexed records, estimated): 1,718,453 - Audio hours (non-unique, estimated): 6,527,883 Audio figures estimate cumulative training exposure, excluding text-only data and pretraining of the base language model and audio encoder. “Unique” counts each indexed record within a source once; the same recording can appear in multiple records or sources, so these are not deduplicated recording hours. **Top-level training dataset families:** - Granary v2: ASR, translation, long-form, contextual biasing, audio QA, transcription style, language identification data - Multi-speaker transcription and associated QA/timestamp variants - Audio-understanding data - Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style data - No-speech abstention data - Text-only instruction-tuning data - PII-aware synthetic ASR data - Nemotron-PII text data **Processing:** Source manifests provide audio references, labels, conversations, and task metadata. The mixture includes human-labeled and pseudo-labeled transcriptions and translations with corresponding instruction prompts. Task-preference sampling selects among transcription, contextual transcription, speech QA, text normalization, captioning, and code-switched targets. **Harmful-content processing:** The training mixture includes text and audio safety-tuning subsets and selected filtered or human-curated components. **Public Summary of Training Content:** - **Granary v2 multilingual speech data:** multilingual data covering ASR, speech translation, contextual and code-switched ASR, speech QA, ITN, captioning, long-form transcription, language identification, PII-aware ASR, and transcript-plus-QA/translation variants. - **Multi-speaker ASR data:** meeting, conversational, and synthetic multi-speaker mixtures, including source material from AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, AMI, ICSI, DiPCo, Fisher/FisherHQ, and Multilingual LibriSpeech. - **Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotation data:** used for paralinguistic event and style-token prediction. - **Audio understanding data:** sound, music, and speech understanding; audio reasoning; spoken instruction following; and safety tuning. Its source families include AudioSet, AudioCaps, Clotho, CochlScene, FSD50K, VGGSound, MusicCaps, NSynth, MELD, MSP-Podcast, CREMA-D, and related audio-instruction mixtures. - **Text-only instruction-tuning data:** instruction following, reasoning, coding, tool use, multilingual, and safety subsets. - **PII-focused data:** Nemotron-PII text SFT plus synthetic PII-aware ASR - **No-speech abstention data:** derived from AudioSet and non-speech audio understanding training data Transcribe's training data includes data licensed from David AI. The DAI-ASR-I18N evaluation set was not part of it. ### Public Datasets The Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe training recipe uses public source datasets both directly and through NVIDIA-created derivatives, including AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, AMI Meeting Corpus, DiPCo, Europarl, Google Speech Commands, ICSI Meeting Corpus, Libri-Light, LibriSpeech, MOSEL, Multilingual LibriSpeech, National Speech Corpus 1 and 6, ReazonSpeech v2, The People's Speech 12k, VCTK, VoxPopuli, and YTC. Additional externally available source families used by the recipe include [Granary v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Granary-v2), Common Voice 26, YODAS2, FLEURS, DUSHA, Golos, M-AILABS, Falar, SOVA, AudioSet, AudioCaps, Clotho, CochlScene, FSD50K, VGGSound, MusicCaps, NSynth, MELD, MSP-Podcast, and CREMA-D. [Nemotron-PII](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-PII) is an NVIDIA-produced synthetic dataset with a public dataset card. ### Private Datasets The training mixture includes the following third-party, vendor-provided, or internally curated source families: - **Third-party speech corpora:** Fisher/FisherHQ, Switchboard, Wall Street Journal, and SPGISpeech - **Vendor-provided multilingual and multi-speaker data:** DavidAI D12a/D12b/D12c and MLC-SLM-2 - **Internal derivative datasets:** multi-speaker task variants, non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotations, PII-aware ASR data, language-identification data, and no-speech abstention data ### Data Crawling and Scraping Some upstream source families are web-derived. These include YODAS/YODAS2 and YTC, as well as publicly available internet scale data represented in AudioSet and related audio-understanding and no-speech datasets. The audio understanding mixture and the pretrained base components may also contain web-derived data. ### Internally Generated Data, Including Prompt-Collected Data NVIDIA-generated or NVIDIA-transformed training artifacts include: - Granary v2 pseudo-transcriptions and model-generated translations, together with human-improved and Riva-labeled variants - Prompt-controlled Granary v2 task expansions for transcription, contextual transcription, speech QA, inverse text normalization, disfluency-reduced transcription, captioning, and code-switched transcription - Fine-, coarse-, distractor-, partial-, and negative-context variants for contextual ASR - Long-form transcription data and transcript-plus-QA, timestamp, speaker-tag, and translation variants - Multi-speaker task formatting and constructed audio mixtures - Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotations - Balanced language-identification prompts and targets - PII tagging and redaction examples - No-speech abstention prompts and empty-response targets - Curated Nemotron text SFT data, audio-instruction, audio-reasoning, and safety-tuning blends Training prompts are developer-authored or generated task instructions associated with prepared training examples. User interactions with a deployed product or model were not used to train the model. ### Self-Sourced Synthetic Data Synthetic and model-generated training data include: - **Nemotron-PII text data:** fully synthetic text examples covering more than 55 PII/PHI categories, with tagged and redacted outputs - **PII-aware ASR data:** synthetic multilingual PII-positive speech examples - **Constructed multi-speaker mixtures:** AuMix examples combining source recordings into conversations of up to eight speakers, including long-form mixtures - **Granary v2 task variants:** generated contextual terms and distractors, speech questions and answers, captions, code-switched targets, and transcript-plus-QA/translation variants - **Audio understanding synthetic-data-generation subsets:** generated captions, questions, answers, instruction-following targets, and reasoning traces for sound, music, speech, and audio-reasoning tasks - **Prompt augmentation:** deterministic and generated prompt variants for transcription, language identification, PII handling, and no-speech abstention Pseudo-labeled ASR and translation examples retain source audio and use model-generated labels; they should not be described as synthetic audio. Constructed multi-speaker mixtures likewise combine source recordings rather than generating new speaker identities. ### Testing Dataset **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Not Applicable **Labeling Method by dataset:** Not Applicable **Properties:** Not Applicable - Testing uses the public benchmark test sets described under [Evaluation Dataset](#evaluation-dataset); there is no separate held-out testing dataset. ### Evaluation Dataset **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Collected, Automated **Labeling Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Labeled, Automatic/Sensors **Properties:** - **Data count:** more than 330,000 test examples from public benchmarks, including approximately 243,000 for English, multilingual, multi-speaker, and contextual transcription; 29,000 for language identification; and 57,000 for audio understanding, voice instruction following, and text-only reasoning. Speech translation, long-form, code-switched, and entity benchmarks are evaluated in addition. - **Modalities:** audio with text instructions, references, and context; text-only for the text reasoning benchmarks. - **Nature of the content:** read speech (LibriSpeech, Multilingual LibriSpeech, FLEURS, Common Voice), parliamentary speech (VoxPopuli), podcasts and online video (GigaSpeech), financial earnings calls (Earnings-22, SPGISpeech), meetings (AMI, NOTSOFAR-1, AISHELL-4, AliMeeting), telephone conversations (CALLHOME), interviews (Mixer 6), noisy and degraded recordings (URGENT 2024), code-switched conversations, spoken questions and instructions (VoiceBench, Spoken-MQA), and speech, sound, and music for audio understanding (MMAU, MMAR, AIR-Bench). - **Linguistic characteristics:** 40 supported languages, with the largest share in English, including Indian-accented English and Hindi (Monsoon), Mandarin meetings, and Hindi–English, Bengali–English, and Mandarin–English code-switching; transcripts are scored both verbatim and in normalized written form, depending on the benchmark. ### Benchmark Results Results are grouped by task. **↓ Lower is better; ↑ higher is better.** Error rates and accuracy are percentages unless another scale is shown. GGML supports both Linux and native Windows. See [hardware, runtime, and operating system compatibility](#software-integration). #### Environment Setup Inference requires **vLLM 0.32.0** and the latest NeMo Speech main branch, which provides the vLLM plugin for this model. Install both into one environment with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and download the checkpoint: ```bash git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech.git nemo-speech cd nemo-speech uv venv --python 3.13 .venv UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$PWD/.venv uv sync --extra asr --extra vllm --locked --no-install-project uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps -e . # PyAV decodes compressed audio formats, such as M4A, without a system FFmpeg. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps av==19.0.2 # vLLM requires OpenCV, which NeMo's dependency settings exclude. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps opencv-python-headless==5.0.0.93 source .venv/bin/activate hf download nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B --local-dir ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B ``` #### Start the Server Start an OpenAI-compatible server on one GPU, with MTP speculative decoding proposing eight tokens (MTP8): ```bash export VLLM_PLUGINS=nemo_speechlm # Allow vLLM to decode recordings up to one hour long (the default is 600 seconds). export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=3600 export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=180 # Word timestamps require the V1 model runner. export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 vllm serve ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --trust-remote-code --dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 \ --max-model-len 65536 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 192 \ --enable-chunked-prefill --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none \ --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --no-async-scheduling \ --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"audio":{"count":6,"length":120000000}}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":8}' \ --reasoning-parser nemotron_v3 \ --trust-request-mm-kwargs \ --middleware nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm.ctc_serving.ctc_timestamp_middleware ``` The server listens on `127.0.0.1:8000`; use `--host` and `--port` to change this. The settings target an H100 with 80 GB of GPU memory; other hardware or workloads may need a different `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-model-len`, or `--max-num-seqs`. The `--middleware` and `--trust-request-mm-kwargs` options let requests opt into [word timestamps](#word-timestamps-and-speaker-diarization). To change the configuration, modify the command as follows: | Configuration | Change | | --- | --- | | Eight GPUs: one data-parallel engine per GPU, with expert parallelism (TP=1, DP=8, EP=8) | Add `--data-parallel-size 8 --api-server-count 8 --enable-expert-parallel --disable-custom-all-reduce` | | MTP with two proposed tokens (MTP2) | Set `"num_speculative_tokens":2` | | No speculative decoding | Remove `--speculative-config` | #### Speculative Decoding Speculative decoding proposes several tokens at once and verifies them with the main model. The checkpoint contains two MTP depths implemented with a repeated layer. MTP8 reuses that layer to propose eight tokens; it does not require eight distinct trained MTP layers. The best mode depends on the GPU and the workload. Approximate throughput for batched English ASR on **one NVIDIA H100 80 GB**, using tuned serving settings: | Decoding mode | Approximate BF16 RTFx | | --- | ---: | | MTP off | Not measured | | MTP2 | 410 | | MTP8 | 270 | | DFlash2 K=7 | 340 | | DFlash2 K=15 | 260 | RTFx is total audio duration divided by processing time: 340 RTFx means about 340 seconds of audio processed per second under batch load. These are rough throughput estimates, excluding server startup, for the English Open ASR and Monsoon datasets with reasoning disabled. Throughput depends on recording length, output length, batch size, and GPU memory settings; it is not a single-request latency estimate. Keep ReplaySSM (`--use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none`) and prefix caching disabled, as in the command above. The first requests after startup are slower while kernels are compiled and warmed up.
DFlash2 draft model As an alternative to MTP, the separate draft model [`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2`](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2) proposes up to 15 tokens at once with vLLM's `dflash` method. DFlash2 and MTP are alternatives and are not combined. K=7 is the recommended starting point; K=15 was slower on the tested ASR workload. vLLM 0.32.0 needs a small fix to its DFlash2 implementation; without it, the server can fail when requests finish. Apply it once to the environment: ```bash python - <<'EOF_PATCH' from pathlib import Path import vllm path = Path(vllm.__file__).parent / "model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py" source = path.read_text() if "safe_anchor_token_ids" not in source: old = " successors = successor_table[candidate_ids]\n" anchor = " anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k)," assert source.count(old) == 1 and source.count(anchor) == 1, "unexpected vLLM version" source = source.replace(old, ( " safe_anchor_token_ids = anchor_token_ids.clamp(\n" " min=0, max=predecessor_table.shape[0] - 1\n" " )\n" + old )).replace(anchor, " safe_anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k),") path.write_text(source) EOF_PATCH ``` The fix modifies vLLM source code (Copyright contributors to the vLLM project), which is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, not under OpenMDW-1.1; see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Then start the server with the following options instead of `--speculative-config` and `--middleware` from the command above. Word timestamps are not available with DFlash2, so the CTC alignment is disabled: ```bash --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","num_speculative_tokens":7,"model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2"}' \ --hf-overrides '{"ctc_timestamps":{"enabled":false}}' ``` vLLM runs DFlash2 only on its V2 model runner, so also run `unset VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER` before starting the server.
#### Send a Request Send audio to the `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint with an OpenAI-compatible client. The following function covers transcription, reasoning, and word timestamps: ```python import base64 from pathlib import Path from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") def ask(audio_path, prompt, system_prompt="", reasoning=False, timestamps=False): audio = base64.b64encode(Path(audio_path).read_bytes()).decode() messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}] if system_prompt else [] messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": f"data:audio/wav;base64,{audio}"}}, ]}) extra_body = { "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": reasoning}, "skip_special_tokens": False, # keep speaker and event tags "spaces_between_special_tokens": False, "seed": 0, } if reasoning: extra_body.update(top_k=-1, thinking_token_budget=17408) extra_body["chat_template_kwargs"]["reasoning_budget"] = 16384 if timestamps: extra_body["mm_processor_kwargs"] = {"capture_ctc_timestamps": True} return client.chat.completions.create( model="nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B", messages=messages, temperature=0.6 if reasoning else 0, top_p=0.95 if reasoning else 1.0, max_tokens=20480 if reasoning else 16384, extra_body=extra_body, ) response = ask("audio.wav", "Transcribe the following audio.") print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` A dense one-hour conversation can need about 20,000 output tokens. For long recordings, raise `max_tokens` or remove it, so that the transcript is not truncated. Transcription uses temperature 0 with reasoning disabled. For audio understanding, enable reasoning and ask a question about the audio: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", "What is happening in this audio?", reasoning=True) ``` This sets temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k disabled, seed 0, a 20,480-token completion limit, and a 16,384-token reasoning budget with a 1,024-token allowance to finish reasoning. Use the task instructions documented under [Evaluation Prompts](#evaluation-prompts) as `prompt` and `system_prompt`. #### Word Timestamps and Speaker Diarization The checkpoint bundles the CTC heads used to align the generated transcript to the audio. With `--middleware` set as in the server command above, request timestamps with `timestamps=True`, together with a speaker-tagged transcription prompt: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. " "Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. " "Write numbers in their standard written form. " "Put speaker tags on the transcription." ), timestamps=True) alignment = response.model_dump()["ctc_timestamps"] if alignment["error"] is not None: raise RuntimeError(alignment["error"]) for word in alignment["words"]: print(word["word"], word["start"], word["end"], word["speaker"]) ``` The response contains a top-level `ctc_timestamps` object: - `words`: word text, start and end times in seconds relative to the input audio, and the transcript's speaker tag. - `diarization`: speaker activity segments derived from the audio. - `speaker_tag_to_diarization_speaker`: the mapping between transcript tags and diarization speakers. - `error`: `null` on success, or an alignment failure reason. Check this field before using the timestamps. Timestamp requests accept one audio recording, `stream=false`, and `n=1`. Keep `skip_special_tokens=false` and ask for speaker tags when speaker attribution is needed. A transcript without speaker tags is aligned as a single speaker. Use the `diarization` segments, rather than word timestamps, when evaluating diarization. ### Evaluation Prompts Use these shortened task-specific templates as starting points. For ASR evaluation, use [Exact ASR Benchmark Prompts](#exact-asr-benchmark-prompts). The ASR benchmark environment uses vLLM 0.28.0 and NeMo Speech with the FP32 preservation change from [PR #16357](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/pull/16357), which is included in the main branch, with MTP2. For audio understanding, spoken instructions, and text reasoning, use [Exact Understanding and Reasoning Prompts](#exact-understanding-and-reasoning-prompts), which lists the complete evaluated system prompts; keep the prepared user questions and choices unchanged. For the remaining benchmark families, use [All Evaluated Prompts](#all-evaluated-prompts), which contains the complete evaluated prompts and reasoning flags. Replace placeholders with the actual languages, labels, or context. #### Prompt Recommendations For these tasks, keep the **system prompt empty**. Send the instruction in the **user message**, alongside the audio. | Task | Recommended user prompt | Why we suggest it | | --- | --- | --- | | Verbatim ASR, including multilingual and long-form audio | `Audio transcription. Language: as spoken. Wording: verbatim, including fillers and repetitions. Formatting: punctuation and capitalization. Output: transcript only.` | Preserves wording and language with an explicit output format. | | Clean written transcript | Replace the wording clause above with `omit fillers and accidental repetitions; keep the remaining spoken wording unchanged`. Add `numbers in their standard written form` if needed. | Makes cleanup and number normalization explicit. | | Speaker attribution / word timestamps | `Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription.` | Provides stable speaker tags for attribution and timestamp alignment; also enable timestamp capture. | | Near-field speaker only (experimental) | `Transcribe this audio. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers as spoken. No punctuation or capitalization. Transcribe only the speaker nearest to the microphone. Do not transcribe any other voices.` | Ignores background voices, such as far-field speech in a meeting room. With LibriSpeech test-clean speech mixed with far-field NOTSOFAR-1 audio, the WER is 4.78% with this prompt and 27.32% with a single-speaker transcription prompt. | | Code-switching / script control | `Transcribe verbatim in the original languages. Preserve hesitations and false starts. Write in

![Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe overview: one speech LLM transcribes a recording in the style selected by the instruction](hero.png) **Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is an open-weight, offline speech and audio model** for transcription in 40 languages, with support for recordings up to one hour and a 65,536-token context. Its hybrid mixture-of-experts architecture activates approximately **4.3B parameters**, including the audio encoder, and it is released in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 precision. [Get started ↓](#quick-start) · [Explore the tasks ↓](#prompt-guide) · [See the evidence ↓](#results-at-a-glance) · [NeMo Speech ↗](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech)
Table of contents - [Model Summary](#model-summary) - [Results at a Glance](#results-at-a-glance) - [Efficiency](#efficiency) - [Quick Start](#quick-start) - [Prompt Guide](#prompt-guide) - [Model Architecture](#model-architecture) - [Language Support Matrix](#language-support-matrix) - [Training, Testing, and Evaluation Datasets](#training-testing-and-evaluation-datasets) - [Benchmark Results](#benchmark-results) - [Inference Setup and Prompts](#inference-setup-and-prompts) - [Ethical Considerations](#ethical-considerations)

# Model Overview ### Description NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe is an offline speech and audio model that processes recordings, together with text instructions and optional context, into text responses. NVIDIA developed this [Speech-Augmented Language Model (SALM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.09424) for multilingual transcription, speech translation, contextual transcription, speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, timestamp prediction, language identification, and audio question answering. The training mixture also includes a small amount of text instruction following and PII tagging/redaction tasks. This model is ready for commercial or non-commercial use. ### Model Summary | | | |:---|:---| | **Total Parameters** | 34B (4.3B active), including the audio encoder | | **Architecture** | Mamba-2–Transformer hybrid Mixture of Experts language model with a Parallel Expert Encoder (Transformer ASR encoder and speaker encoder) | | **Precision** | BF16 (full-precision reference weights); [FP8](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-FP8) and [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-NVFP4) variants are available | | **Context Length** | 65,536 tokens; recordings up to 1 hour | | **Inputs / Outputs** | Audio and text / text, with optional word timestamps | | **Languages** | 40; see the [language support matrix](#language-support-matrix) | | **Tasks** | Transcription in verbatim or written form, contextual transcription, speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, speech translation, language identification, and audio question answering | | **Deployment** | 1× H100 80 GB; see the [hardware compatibility table](#software-integration) | | **Speculative Decoding** | Native Multi-Token Prediction (MTP); optional DFlash2 draft model | | **Reasoning Mode** | Configurable through the chat template (`enable_thinking=True/False`) | | **Recommended Sampling** | Transcription, translation, and language identification: temperature 0, reasoning off; audio understanding: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, reasoning on | | **Best For** | Highest accuracy, customization, and fine-tuning | | **License** | [OpenMDW-1.1](https://openmdw.ai/license/1-1/) | ### Results at a Glance Results captured on October 12, 2026. Error rates are percentages. **↓ Lower is better.** Complete results are listed under [Benchmark Results](#benchmark-results). **Best published results** | Capability | Benchmark | Metric | Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe | Next best published | |:---|:---|:---|:---|:---| | Multi-speaker ASR | AMI, CALLHOME, Mixer 6, NOTSOFAR-1 full sessions | Mean cpWER ↓ | **15.80** | DiCoW v3.3 + DiariZen 16.83 | | Style control | Preference-ASR | WER ↓, default / instructed | **7.56 / 6.16** | Canary-Qwen 8.16 / 8.36 | **Best open-weight results** | Capability | Benchmark | Metric | Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe | Next best open-weight model | |:---|:---|:---|:---|:---| | English ASR | Open ASR Leaderboard, 9 public sets | Mean WER ↓ | **4.71** | Qwen3-ASR-1.7B 4.94 | | Long-form ASR | Open ASR Leaderboard, long-form | Mean WER ↓ | **10.98** | Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 13.37 | | Multilingual ASR | Multilingual Open ASR Leaderboard, 7 languages | Mean WER ↓ | **4.62** | Qwen3-ASR-1.7B 6.49 | ### Efficiency ![Throughput versus median request latency of the Nemotron Transcribe NIM on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU for BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 with and without speculative decoding](serving_performance.png) With the optimized vLLM implementation in the Nemotron Transcribe NIM, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU transcribes up to 2,238 seconds of audio per second (NVFP4 with DFlash2 speculative decoding) and returns the transcript of a 30-second recording in 0.13 seconds. These serving optimizations are not yet part of the open-source release; we aim to upstream them to NeMo Speech and vLLM at a later date. The vLLM integration shipped in NeMo Speech on the release day is intended for model development and is expected to be roughly two times slower. ### Quick Start The example below serves this checkpoint on **one H100 80 GB** with vLLM 0.32.0 and the latest NeMo Speech main branch. Install both and download the checkpoint as described in [Environment Setup](#environment-setup). ```bash export VLLM_PLUGINS=nemo_speechlm export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=3600 export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=180 # Word timestamps require the V1 model runner. export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 vllm serve ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --trust-remote-code --dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 \ --max-model-len 65536 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 192 \ --enable-chunked-prefill --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none \ --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --no-async-scheduling \ --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"audio":{"count":6,"length":120000000}}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":8}' \ --reasoning-parser nemotron_v3 \ --trust-request-mm-kwargs \ --middleware nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm.ctc_serving.ctc_timestamp_middleware ``` Once the server has loaded the model, transcribe a recording: ```python import base64 from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") audio = base64.b64encode(open("audio.wav", "rb").read()).decode() response = client.chat.completions.create( model="nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "Transcribe the following audio."}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": f"data:audio/wav;base64,{audio}"}}, ]}], temperature=0, extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}, "skip_special_tokens": False}, ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` See [Inference Setup and Prompts](#inference-setup-and-prompts) for other configurations, reasoning, word timestamps, and task-specific prompts. ### Prompt Guide Choose the transcription style with the instruction in the user message; keep the system prompt empty for transcription and translation. | What you need | What to ask for | Where it fits | |:---|:---|:---| | The words as spoken | `Audio transcription. Language: as spoken. Wording: verbatim, including fillers and repetitions. Formatting: punctuation and capitalization. Output: transcript only.` | Research transcripts and detailed review | | Readable text | `Audio transcription. Language: as spoken. Wording: omit fillers and accidental repetitions; keep the remaining spoken wording unchanged. Formatting: punctuation and capitalization. Output: transcript only.` | Captions, notes, and searchable recordings | | Domain vocabulary | `Transcribe with punctuation and capitalization. Context terms: .` | Earnings calls, support recordings, and technical discussions | | Who said what, and when | `Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription.` Enable word timestamps in the request. | Meeting review and editing workflows | | Only the person at the microphone (experimental) | `Transcribe this audio. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers as spoken. No punctuation or capitalization. Transcribe only the speaker nearest to the microphone. Do not transcribe any other voices.` | Dictation and voice interfaces with background speakers | | Speech in another language | `Please translate the given speech to .` | Multilingual media and localization | | An answer from the recording | Ask a specific question about the audio and enable reasoning. | Audio search, review, and understanding | **This is an offline model.** Internal audio chunking does not make it a real-time streaming ASR service. Language and task support vary; check the [language support matrix](#language-support-matrix). See [Prompt Recommendations](#prompt-recommendations) for more tasks and [All Evaluated Prompts](#all-evaluated-prompts) for the exact benchmark prompts. ### License / Terms of Use Use of this model is governed by the [OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1 (OpenMDW-1.1)](https://openmdw.ai/license/1-1/). Users are responsible for complying with this license and with any third-party licenses or notices applicable to components included in the distributed model materials. ### Deployment Geography Global ### Use Case Intended users are developers and researchers building speech interfaces, transcription and translation tools, meeting and media processing, customer-service analytics, and audio-understanding applications. Text context can supply task instructions and vocabulary hints. Speaker labels are intended to distinguish speakers within a recording; they do not establish real-world identity. ### Release Date - Build.Nvidia.com 10/28/2026 - Github 10/28/2026 via [NVIDIA NeMo Speech](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/NeMo/) - Hugging Face 10/28/2026 via [NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B) - NGC 10/28/2026 via [NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B](https://registry.ngc.nvidia.com/orgs/0767305323357365/teams/transcribe-3_5-ea/models/nvidia-nemotron-3-5-transcribe-30b-a4b) ## References - Model page: [NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B) - Technical report: [Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe Technical Report](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-Technical-Report.pdf) - Base language model: [NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B BF16](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16) - Quick-start and inference documentation: see [Inference quick start guide](#inference-setup-and-prompts). ## Model Architecture ![Architecture of Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: a Parallel Expert Encoder with ASR and diarization branches feeds the hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE language model, with MTP and CTC timestamp heads](architecture.png) **Architecture Type:** Other - hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model with a Transformer audio encoder **Network Architecture:** Nemotron 3.5 Lightning hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE with Transformer ASR encoder and Sortformer speaker encoder **Design:** Audio perception module consisting of transformer ASR encoder and [Nemotron-3-Diarization](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization) speaker encoder, a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) timestamp alignment head, and [NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16) language backbone. The perception configuration uses a 1,280-dimensional identity connector followed by a learned projection to 2,688 dimensions. Audio features are combined with the text prompt for text generation. The model enables joint multi-token prediction (MTP), with two trained next-token prediction depths using a repeated layer and retaining the existing head. Reusing the repeated layer during inference supports up to eight speculative tokens. A dedicated [DFlash2](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2) draft model, a block-diffusion drafter based on DFlash, is also provided as an option for speculative decoding. **Base model:** [`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16`](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16); 600M parameter pretrained ASR transformer; and approximately 99M parameter Nemotron-3-Diarization speaker encoder. **Parameter count:** The language backbone has approximately 3.5B active parameters. Together with the approximately 800M-parameter joint audio encoder, the model has approximately 4.3B active parameters. **Precision:** Weights are released in bfloat16 (BF16), with FP8 and NVFP4 quantized variants. ## Language Support Matrix - ✓ Supported - — Not specified ASR means automatic speech recognition; code-switching means using more than one language within a recording. Translation support covers both directions between English and the listed language. Regional variants listed in parentheses are supported as part of their language. The matrix covers transcription and translation. Text: String (plain text or chat messages). | | Parameters | Audio: one-dimensional waveform per processed channel. Text: one-dimensional token sequence. | | Sampling and preprocessing | Recipe audio sampling rate: 16 kHz. Use the exported model's preprocessor and `nemotron3p5` prompt format. Encoder feature stride is configured as approximately 80 ms per audio token equivalent. | | Limits | The model is trained with recordings up to 1 hour long, and its maximum context size in training was 65536 tokens. It is not guaranteed to generalize beyond these limits. | | Audio chunking | The encoder uses 30-second post-feature chunks. This is an internal processing choice, not a 30-second recording limit or a streaming latency claim. | | Language coverage | See the [40-language support matrix](#language-support-matrix). | **Other Properties Related to Input:** The model processes 16kHz single-channel audio decoded to a float32 PCM waveform. The maximum supported audio length is up to 1 hour. ## Outputs | Property | Specification | | --- | --- | | Types | Text. | | Formats | String. | | Parameters | One-dimensional (1D) token sequence. | | Content | Depending on the prompt: transcripts, translations, speaker/event tags, language labels, answers, or PII annotations/redactions. | **Optional structured output:** With timestamp capture enabled in vLLM (an open-source LLM inference and serving engine), the response also includes a `ctc_timestamps` object containing word text, start and end times in seconds relative to the input audio, speaker tags, diarization segments, a mapping from transcript speaker tags to diarization speakers, and an alignment-error field. See [Word Timestamps and Speaker Diarization](#word-timestamps-and-speaker-diarization). **Other Properties Related to Output:** Punctuation, normalization, speaker attribution, and event annotations depend on the task and prompt. Our AI models are designed and/or optimized to run on NVIDIA GPU-accelerated systems. By leveraging NVIDIA's hardware (e.g. GPU cores) and software frameworks (e.g., CUDA libraries), the model achieves faster training and inference times compared to CPU-only solutions. ## Software Integration **Runtime Engine(s):** Training is done with [NeMo Speech](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/NeMo/) with the [NeMo Automodel](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Automodel) backend, PyTorch, and a Lhotse dataloader. [AIStore](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aistore) was used for data storage throughout the model development. The recipe uses Transformer Engine attention/linear kernels, grouped GEMM experts, and DeepEP dispatch. Inference is done with SpeechLM-enabled vLLM with NeMo Skills orchestration. **vLLM inference software:** vLLM **0.32.0** and the latest NeMo Speech main branch. Use the [inference setup](#environment-setup). **Operating systems:** Linux and Windows. Linux runtimes can also run on Windows through WSL2.
