Following the V-model methodology, iterative testing and validation at both unit and system levels are essential to mitigate risks, meet technical and functional requirements, and ensure compliance with safety and ethical standards before deployment. ## Model Version(s) - NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B (BF16) - [NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-FP8](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-FP8) and [NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-NVFP4): post-training quantized variants; see the hardware compatibility table above to choose a precision supported by your GPU - [NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2): optional draft model for speculative decoding The model can be integrated into an AI system as a service, through the OpenAI-compatible API of a vLLM server, or in-process, with Hugging Face Transformers or, on supported GPUs, with GGML (see the [Inference quick start guide](#inference-setup-and-prompts)). It can be adapted to new domains and tasks with the fine-tuning toolkit in [NeMo Speech](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/tree/main/examples/speechlm2/finetuning). ## Checkpoint Contents The Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe checkpoint includes the CTC heads and speaker encoder used for word timestamps and speaker diarization. ## Training, Testing, and Evaluation Datasets ### Training Dataset **Data Modality:** Audio, Text **Audio Training Data Size:** More than 1 Million Hours (approximately 1.72 million hours across unique indexed audio examples; 6.53 million hours including repeated exposure) **Text Training Data Size:** 1 Billion to 10 Trillion Tokens (5.6 billion unique tokens) **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Collected, Automated, Synthetic **Labeling Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Labeled, Automatic/Sensors, Synthetic **Properties:** Approximately 372 million unique audio examples (1.72 million hours) and 5.6 billion unique text tokens. Audio is paired with text instructions and targets: transcripts, translations, speaker-attributed transcripts, captions, answers, and labels; a small share of the data is text-only. The content comprises public and third-party speech corpora (read speech, conversations, meetings, broadcasts, and earnings calls), web-derived speech, sound, and music, pseudo-labeled transcripts and translations, constructed multi-speaker mixtures, and synthetic data such as synthetic PII text and speech. The data covers the 40 supported languages, with the largest share in English, as well as code-switched speech. #### Training Data Size Details **Total examples, audio hours, text tokens, unique dataset count, partition percentages, and collection periods:** - Total multimodal tokens (non-unique): 479 billion - Audio share of multimodal input positions: approx. 60% - Audio tokens (non-unique): 286 billion - Text tokens (non-unique, including responses to audio examples): 193 billion - Audio examples (unique indexed records, estimated): 372,206,279 - Audio examples (non-unique, estimated): 1,780,012,724 - Audio hours (unique indexed records, estimated): 1,718,453 - Audio hours (non-unique, estimated): 6,527,883 Audio figures estimate cumulative training exposure, excluding text-only data and pretraining of the base language model and audio encoder. “Unique” counts each indexed record within a source once; the same recording can appear in multiple records or sources, so these are not deduplicated recording hours. **Top-level training dataset families:** - Granary v2: ASR, translation, long-form, contextual biasing, audio QA, transcription style, language identification data - Multi-speaker transcription and associated QA/timestamp variants - Audio-understanding data - Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style data - No-speech abstention data - Text-only instruction-tuning data - PII-aware synthetic ASR data - Nemotron-PII text data **Processing:** Source manifests provide audio references, labels, conversations, and task metadata. The mixture includes human-labeled and pseudo-labeled transcriptions and translations with corresponding instruction prompts. Task-preference sampling selects among transcription, contextual transcription, speech QA, text normalization, captioning, and code-switched targets. **Harmful-content processing:** The training mixture includes text and audio safety-tuning subsets and selected filtered or human-curated components. **Public Summary of Training Content:** - **Granary v2 multilingual speech data:** multilingual data covering ASR, speech translation, contextual and code-switched ASR, speech QA, ITN, captioning, long-form transcription, language identification, PII-aware ASR, and transcript-plus-QA/translation variants. - **Multi-speaker ASR data:** meeting, conversational, and synthetic multi-speaker mixtures, including source material from AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, AMI, ICSI, DiPCo, Fisher/FisherHQ, and Multilingual LibriSpeech. - **Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotation data:** used for paralinguistic event and style-token prediction. - **Audio understanding data:** sound, music, and speech understanding; audio reasoning; spoken instruction following; and safety tuning. Its source families include AudioSet, AudioCaps, Clotho, CochlScene, FSD50K, VGGSound, MusicCaps, NSynth, MELD, MSP-Podcast, CREMA-D, and related audio-instruction mixtures. - **Text-only instruction-tuning data:** instruction following, reasoning, coding, tool use, multilingual, and safety subsets. - **PII-focused data:** Nemotron-PII text SFT plus synthetic PII-aware ASR - **No-speech abstention data:** derived from AudioSet and non-speech audio understanding training data Transcribe's training data includes data licensed from David AI. The DAI-ASR-I18N evaluation set was not part of it. ### Public Datasets The Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe training recipe uses public source datasets both directly and through NVIDIA-created derivatives, including AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, AMI Meeting Corpus, DiPCo, Europarl, Google Speech Commands, ICSI Meeting Corpus, Libri-Light, LibriSpeech, MOSEL, Multilingual LibriSpeech, National Speech Corpus 1 and 6, ReazonSpeech v2, The People's Speech 12k, VCTK, VoxPopuli, and YTC. Additional externally available source families used by the recipe include [Granary v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Granary-v2), Common Voice 26, YODAS2, FLEURS, DUSHA, Golos, M-AILABS, Falar, SOVA, AudioSet, AudioCaps, Clotho, CochlScene, FSD50K, VGGSound, MusicCaps, NSynth, MELD, MSP-Podcast, and CREMA-D. [Nemotron-PII](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-PII) is an NVIDIA-produced synthetic dataset with a public dataset card. ### Private Datasets The training mixture includes the following third-party, vendor-provided, or internally curated source families: - **Third-party speech corpora:** Fisher/FisherHQ, Switchboard, Wall Street Journal, and SPGISpeech - **Vendor-provided multilingual and multi-speaker data:** DavidAI D12a/D12b/D12c and MLC-SLM-2 - **Internal derivative datasets:** multi-speaker task variants, non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotations, PII-aware ASR data, language-identification data, and no-speech abstention data ### Data Crawling and Scraping Some upstream source families are web-derived. These include YODAS/YODAS2 and YTC, as well as publicly available internet scale data represented in AudioSet and related audio-understanding and no-speech datasets. The audio understanding mixture and the pretrained base components may also contain web-derived data. ### Internally Generated Data, Including Prompt-Collected Data NVIDIA-generated or NVIDIA-transformed training artifacts include: - Granary v2 pseudo-transcriptions and model-generated translations, together with human-improved and Riva-labeled variants - Prompt-controlled Granary v2 task expansions for transcription, contextual transcription, speech QA, inverse text normalization, disfluency-reduced transcription, captioning, and code-switched transcription - Fine-, coarse-, distractor-, partial-, and negative-context variants for contextual ASR - Long-form transcription data and transcript-plus-QA, timestamp, speaker-tag, and translation variants - Multi-speaker task formatting and constructed audio mixtures - Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotations - Balanced language-identification prompts and targets - PII tagging and redaction examples - No-speech abstention prompts and empty-response targets - Curated Nemotron text SFT data, audio-instruction, audio-reasoning, and safety-tuning blends Training prompts are developer-authored or generated task instructions associated with prepared training examples. User interactions with a deployed product or model were not used to train the model. ### Self-Sourced Synthetic Data Synthetic and model-generated training data include: - **Nemotron-PII text data:** fully synthetic text examples covering more than 55 PII/PHI categories, with tagged and redacted outputs - **PII-aware ASR data:** synthetic multilingual PII-positive speech examples - **Constructed multi-speaker mixtures:** AuMix examples combining source recordings into conversations of up to eight speakers, including long-form mixtures - **Granary v2 task variants:** generated contextual terms and distractors, speech questions and answers, captions, code-switched targets, and transcript-plus-QA/translation variants - **Audio understanding synthetic-data-generation subsets:** generated captions, questions, answers, instruction-following targets, and reasoning traces for sound, music, speech, and audio-reasoning tasks - **Prompt augmentation:** deterministic and generated prompt variants for transcription, language identification, PII handling, and no-speech abstention Pseudo-labeled ASR and translation examples retain source audio and use model-generated labels; they should not be described as synthetic audio. Constructed multi-speaker mixtures likewise combine source recordings rather than generating new speaker identities. ### Testing Dataset **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Not Applicable **Labeling Method by dataset:** Not Applicable **Properties:** Not Applicable - Testing uses the public benchmark test sets described under [Evaluation Dataset](#evaluation-dataset); there is no separate held-out testing dataset. ### Evaluation Dataset **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Collected, Automated **Labeling Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Labeled, Automatic/Sensors **Properties:** - **Data count:** more than 330,000 test examples from public benchmarks, including approximately 243,000 for English, multilingual, multi-speaker, and contextual transcription; 29,000 for language identification; and 57,000 for audio understanding, voice instruction following, and text-only reasoning. Speech translation, long-form, code-switched, and entity benchmarks are evaluated in addition. - **Modalities:** audio with text instructions, references, and context; text-only for the text reasoning benchmarks. - **Nature of the content:** read speech (LibriSpeech, Multilingual LibriSpeech, FLEURS, Common Voice), parliamentary speech (VoxPopuli), podcasts and online video (GigaSpeech), financial earnings calls (Earnings-22, SPGISpeech), meetings (AMI, NOTSOFAR-1, AISHELL-4, AliMeeting), telephone conversations (CALLHOME), interviews (Mixer 6), noisy and degraded recordings (URGENT 2024), code-switched conversations, spoken questions and instructions (VoiceBench, Spoken-MQA), and speech, sound, and music for audio understanding (MMAU, MMAR, AIR-Bench). - **Linguistic characteristics:** 40 supported languages, with the largest share in English, including Indian-accented English and Hindi (Monsoon), Mandarin meetings, and Hindi–English, Bengali–English, and Mandarin–English code-switching; transcripts are scored both verbatim and in normalized written form, depending on the benchmark. ### Benchmark Results Results are grouped by task. **↓ Lower is better; ↑ higher is better.** Error rates and accuracy are percentages unless another scale is shown. GGML supports both Linux and native Windows. See [hardware, runtime, and operating system compatibility](#software-integration). #### Environment Setup Inference requires **vLLM 0.32.0** and the latest NeMo Speech main branch, which provides the vLLM plugin for this model. Install both into one environment with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and download the checkpoint: ```bash git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech.git nemo-speech cd nemo-speech uv venv --python 3.13 .venv UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$PWD/.venv uv sync --extra asr --extra vllm --locked --no-install-project uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps -e . # PyAV decodes compressed audio formats, such as M4A, without a system FFmpeg. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps av==19.0.2 # vLLM requires OpenCV, which NeMo's dependency settings exclude. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps opencv-python-headless==5.0.0.93 source .venv/bin/activate hf download nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B --local-dir ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B ``` #### Start the Server Start an OpenAI-compatible server on one GPU, with MTP speculative decoding proposing eight tokens (MTP8): ```bash export VLLM_PLUGINS=nemo_speechlm # Allow vLLM to decode recordings up to one hour long (the default is 600 seconds). export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=3600 export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=180 # Word timestamps require the V1 model runner. export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 vllm serve ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --trust-remote-code --dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 \ --max-model-len 65536 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 192 \ --enable-chunked-prefill --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none \ --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --no-async-scheduling \ --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"audio":{"count":6,"length":120000000}}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":8}' \ --reasoning-parser nemotron_v3 \ --trust-request-mm-kwargs \ --middleware nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm.ctc_serving.ctc_timestamp_middleware ``` The server listens on `127.0.0.1:8000`; use `--host` and `--port` to change this. The settings target an H100 with 80 GB of GPU memory; other hardware or workloads may need a different `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-model-len`, or `--max-num-seqs`. The `--middleware` and `--trust-request-mm-kwargs` options let requests opt into [word timestamps](#word-timestamps-and-speaker-diarization). To change the configuration, modify the command as follows: | Configuration | Change | | --- | --- | | Eight GPUs: one data-parallel engine per GPU, with expert parallelism (TP=1, DP=8, EP=8) | Add `--data-parallel-size 8 --api-server-count 8 --enable-expert-parallel --disable-custom-all-reduce` | | MTP with two proposed tokens (MTP2) | Set `"num_speculative_tokens":2` | | No speculative decoding | Remove `--speculative-config` | #### Speculative Decoding Speculative decoding proposes several tokens at once and verifies them with the main model. The checkpoint contains two MTP depths implemented with a repeated layer. MTP8 reuses that layer to propose eight tokens; it does not require eight distinct trained MTP layers. The best mode depends on the GPU and the workload. Approximate throughput for batched English ASR on **one NVIDIA H100 80 GB**, using tuned serving settings: | Decoding mode | Approximate BF16 RTFx | | --- | ---: | | MTP off | Not measured | | MTP2 | 410 | | MTP8 | 270 | | DFlash2 K=7 | 340 | | DFlash2 K=15 | 260 | RTFx is total audio duration divided by processing time: 340 RTFx means about 340 seconds of audio processed per second under batch load. These are rough throughput estimates, excluding server startup, for the English Open ASR and Monsoon datasets with reasoning disabled. Throughput depends on recording length, output length, batch size, and GPU memory settings; it is not a single-request latency estimate. Keep ReplaySSM (`--use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none`) and prefix caching disabled, as in the command above. The first requests after startup are slower while kernels are compiled and warmed up.
DFlash2 draft model As an alternative to MTP, the separate draft model [`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2`](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2) proposes up to 15 tokens at once with vLLM's `dflash` method. DFlash2 and MTP are alternatives and are not combined. K=7 is the recommended starting point; K=15 was slower on the tested ASR workload. vLLM 0.32.0 needs a small fix to its DFlash2 implementation; without it, the server can fail when requests finish. Apply it once to the environment: ```bash python - <<'EOF_PATCH' from pathlib import Path import vllm path = Path(vllm.__file__).parent / "model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py" source = path.read_text() if "safe_anchor_token_ids" not in source: old = " successors = successor_table[candidate_ids]\n" anchor = " anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k)," assert source.count(old) == 1 and source.count(anchor) == 1, "unexpected vLLM version" source = source.replace(old, ( " safe_anchor_token_ids = anchor_token_ids.clamp(\n" " min=0, max=predecessor_table.shape[0] - 1\n" " )\n" + old )).replace(anchor, " safe_anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k),") path.write_text(source) EOF_PATCH ``` The fix modifies vLLM source code (Copyright contributors to the vLLM project), which is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, not under OpenMDW-1.1; see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Then start the server with the following options instead of `--speculative-config` and `--middleware` from the command above. Word timestamps are not available with DFlash2, so the CTC alignment is disabled: ```bash --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","num_speculative_tokens":7,"model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2"}' \ --hf-overrides '{"ctc_timestamps":{"enabled":false}}' ``` vLLM runs DFlash2 only on its V2 model runner, so also run `unset VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER` before starting the server.
#### Send a Request Send audio to the `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint with an OpenAI-compatible client. The following function covers transcription, reasoning, and word timestamps: ```python import base64 from pathlib import Path from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") def ask(audio_path, prompt, system_prompt="", reasoning=False, timestamps=False): audio = base64.b64encode(Path(audio_path).read_bytes()).decode() messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}] if system_prompt else [] messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": f"data:audio/wav;base64,{audio}"}}, ]}) extra_body = { "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": reasoning}, "skip_special_tokens": False, # keep speaker and event tags "spaces_between_special_tokens": False, "seed": 0, } if reasoning: extra_body.update(top_k=-1, thinking_token_budget=17408) extra_body["chat_template_kwargs"]["reasoning_budget"] = 16384 if timestamps: extra_body["mm_processor_kwargs"] = {"capture_ctc_timestamps": True} return client.chat.completions.create( model="nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B", messages=messages, temperature=0.6 if reasoning else 0, top_p=0.95 if reasoning else 1.0, max_tokens=20480 if reasoning else 16384, extra_body=extra_body, ) response = ask("audio.wav", "Transcribe the following audio.") print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` A dense one-hour conversation can need about 20,000 output tokens. For long recordings, raise `max_tokens` or remove it, so that the transcript is not truncated. Transcription uses temperature 0 with reasoning disabled. For audio understanding, enable reasoning and ask a question about the audio: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", "What is happening in this audio?", reasoning=True) ``` This sets temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k disabled, seed 0, a 20,480-token completion limit, and a 16,384-token reasoning budget with a 1,024-token allowance to finish reasoning. Use the task instructions documented under [Evaluation Prompts](#evaluation-prompts) as `prompt` and `system_prompt`. #### Word Timestamps and Speaker Diarization The checkpoint bundles the CTC heads used to align the generated transcript to the audio. With `--middleware` set as in the server command above, request timestamps with `timestamps=True`, together with a speaker-tagged transcription prompt: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. " "Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. " "Write numbers in their standard written form. " "Put speaker tags on the transcription." ), timestamps=True) alignment = response.model_dump()["ctc_timestamps"] if alignment["error"] is not None: raise RuntimeError(alignment["error"]) for word in alignment["words"]: print(word["word"], word["start"], word["end"], word["speaker"]) ``` The response contains a top-level `ctc_timestamps` object: - `words`: word text, start and end times in seconds relative to the input audio, and the transcript's speaker tag. - `diarization`: speaker activity segments derived from the audio. - `speaker_tag_to_diarization_speaker`: the mapping between transcript tags and diarization speakers. - `error`: `null` on success, or an alignment failure reason. Check this field before using the timestamps. Timestamp requests accept one audio recording, `stream=false`, and `n=1`. Keep `skip_special_tokens=false` and ask for speaker tags when speaker attribution is needed. A transcript without speaker tags is aligned as a single speaker. Use the `diarization` segments, rather than word timestamps, when evaluating diarization. ### Evaluation Prompts Use these shortened task-specific templates as starting points. For ASR evaluation, use [Exact ASR Benchmark Prompts](#exact-asr-benchmark-prompts). The ASR benchmark environment uses vLLM 0.28.0 and NeMo Speech with the FP32 preservation change from [PR #16357](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/pull/16357), which is included in the main branch, with MTP2. For audio understanding, spoken instructions, and text reasoning, use [Exact Understanding and Reasoning Prompts](#exact-understanding-and-reasoning-prompts), which lists the complete evaluated system prompts; keep the prepared user questions and choices unchanged. For the remaining benchmark families, use [All Evaluated Prompts](#all-evaluated-prompts), which contains the complete evaluated prompts and reasoning flags. Replace placeholders with the actual languages, labels, or context. #### Prompt Recommendations For these tasks, keep the **system prompt empty**. Send the instruction in the **user message**, alongside the audio. | Task | Recommended user prompt | Why we suggest it | | --- | --- | --- | | Verbatim ASR, including multilingual and long-form audio | `Audio transcription. Language: as spoken. Wording: verbatim, including fillers and repetitions. Formatting: punctuation and capitalization. Output: transcript only.` | Preserves wording and language with an explicit output format. | | Clean written transcript | Replace the wording clause above with `omit fillers and accidental repetitions; keep the remaining spoken wording unchanged`. Add `numbers in their standard written form` if needed. | Makes cleanup and number normalization explicit. | | Speaker attribution / word timestamps | `Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription.` | Provides stable speaker tags for attribution and timestamp alignment; also enable timestamp capture. | | Near-field speaker only (experimental) | `Transcribe this audio. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers as spoken. No punctuation or capitalization. Transcribe only the speaker nearest to the microphone. Do not transcribe any other voices.` | Ignores background voices, such as far-field speech in a meeting room. With LibriSpeech test-clean speech mixed with far-field NOTSOFAR-1 audio, the WER is 4.78% with this prompt and 27.32% with a single-speaker transcription prompt. | | Code-switching / script control | `Transcribe verbatim in the original languages. Preserve hesitations and false starts. Write in

# RubatoCodec

[![Code: GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/Code-GitHub-black?logo=github)](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec)
[![Paper: arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.29434-b31b1b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29434)
[![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue)](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)

RubatoCodec is a neural speech codec that divides speech into a fixed number of
variable-duration events. Each event carries discrete code indices and an
explicit duration. Event placement adapts to speech content, while the number of
events is determined exactly by the utterance length, so the token sequence
length a speech generator must produce is predictable. A causal decoder renders
completed events incrementally, which makes the codec suitable for streaming
text-to-speech.

The name comes from the musical term *rubato*: local timing flexes while the
overall tempo is preserved.

- **Adaptive Firing with an exact event budget.** Multi-scale latent
  dissimilarity and waveform spectral flux guide cumulative allocation on a
  50-Hz latent grid. For `T` frames the event count is exactly
  `max(1, min(T, round(0.25 · T)))`, giving 12.5 events/s. No learned boundary
  predictor, boundary labels, or rate loss is used.
- **Streaming decoding.** Events can be decoded one at a time or in chunks.
  Event-by-event decoding takes about 11 ms per event on an NVIDIA H200, well
  below the ~80 ms of audio each event represents on average.
- **Hybrid residual quantizer with depth control.** A semantically supervised
  FSQ first layer is followed by 15 DAC-style residual VQ layers, each with
  4,096 entries. Any prefix depth from 1 to 16 can be decoded, giving code-index
  bitrates of 0.15–2.4 kbit/s plus duration information.
- **Multilingual.** Trained on approximately 375,000 hours of speech, mostly
  English, Japanese, and Chinese, with 16-kHz input and 44.1-kHz output.

![RubatoCodec architecture](assets/architecture.png)

## Model details

| | |
|---|---|
| Input / output sample rate | 16 kHz / 44.1 kHz |
| Latent grid | 50 Hz |
| Event rate | 12.5 events/s (retention ratio 0.25) |
| Quantizer | 16 layers × 4,096 entries; layer 0 FSQ with semantic distillation, layers 1–15 residual VQ |
| Bitrate | 1.23 kbit/s at depth 8, 2.43 kbit/s at depth 16 (LibriSpeech, including duration information) |
| Decoder | Fully causal Transformer + ISTFT head, streaming capable |
| Parameters | 246M codec (72M encoder, 173M decoder, 1M quantizer) + frozen [w2v-BERT 2.0](https://huggingface.co/facebook/w2v-bert-2.0) (580M, encoding only) |
| License | Apache 2.0 |

## Usage

Install the package from the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec
cd RubatoCodec
uv sync
```

Encode and decode:

```python
import soundfile as sf
import torch

from rubatocodec import RubatoCodec

codec = RubatoCodec.from_pretrained("third-intelligence/RubatoCodec", device="cuda")

data, sr = sf.read("speech.wav", dtype="float32")  # mono waveform
wav = torch.from_numpy(data)

enc = codec.encode(wav, sr=sr)       # {"codes": (16, K) int64, "durs": (K,) int64}
audio = codec.decode(enc)            # (1, 1, T_audio) at 44.1 kHz, full depth
audio = codec.decode(enc, depth=8)   # lower bitrate with the first 8 layers

sf.write("recon.wav", audio[0, 0].cpu().numpy(), codec.output_sr)
```

`durs` gives each event's duration in 20-ms grid frames. Loading also downloads
`facebook/w2v-bert-2.0`, which is used only for encoding.

Streaming decoding, inference settings, the code format, and training are
documented in the repository:
[inference guide](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/inference.md),
[architecture](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/architecture.md),
[training](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/training.md).

## Evaluation

RubatoCodec is evaluated on LibriSpeech test-clean, VCTK, JVS nonpara30, JVNV,
and seed-tts-eval test-zh against 13 other codecs. At comparable bitrates, it
shows the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the
English and Japanese benchmarks and high predicted quality, while the strongest
comparators achieve higher PESQ-WB and STOI.

dWER/dCER compare ASR transcripts of the reconstructed and original audio
(Whisper-large-v3 for English and Japanese, Paraformer-zh for Mandarin). SIM is
cosine similarity of speaker embeddings from a fine-tuned WavLM-Large speaker verification model. Bitrates include duration information.

The tables below show a subset of the compared codecs. **Bold** and
<ins>underline</ins> mark the best and second-best scores within each bitrate
band.

**Quality versus bitrate** (RubatoCodec is marked with a red star)

![English reconstruction versus bitrate](assets/english_reconstruction.png)

![Japanese and Mandarin reconstruction versus bitrate](assets/multilingual_reconstruction.png)

**Adaptive event placement.** Each rectangle in the lower strip is one event.
Longer events cover pauses and low-energy regions, while speech receives
shorter events, with the same 12.5 events/s budget in every utterance.

![Adaptive event placement on English, Japanese, and Mandarin speech](assets/codec_firing_examples.png)

The full protocol, all compared codecs and operating points, and throughput
measurements are in the
[evaluation document](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/evaluation.md)
and the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29434).

## Training data

Approximately 375,000 hours of public and internal speech. Public sources include
[Emilia-YODAS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/amphion/Emilia-Dataset),
[HiFiTTS-2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/hifitts-2) (44-kHz subset),
[ReazonSpeech](https://huggingface.co/datasets/reazon-research/reazonspeech),
[The People's Speech](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MLCommons/peoples_speech)
(excluding ShareAlike-licensed data),
[VoxPopuli](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/voxpopuli),
[Multilingual LibriSpeech](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/multilingual_librispeech)
(excluding English),
[Omnilingual ASR Corpus](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/omnilingual-asr-corpus),
and [IndicVoices](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4bharat/IndicVoices). English, Japanese,
and Chinese account for approximately 44%, 27%, and 13% of the data, and other
languages for the remaining 16%.

## Limitations

- RubatoCodec is trained on speech only and is intended for speech. It is not
  designed for music or general audio.
- Encoding requires the whole utterance, because the event budget is defined at
  the utterance level. Only decoding is streaming.
- Signal-fidelity metrics (PESQ-WB, STOI) are below those of the strongest
  compared codecs at similar bitrates.
- Evaluation covers English, Japanese, and Mandarin, all of which appear in the
  training data. Performance on other languages has not been evaluated.
- Like other speech codecs, RubatoCodec can be used in speech generation systems
  capable of voice cloning. Do not use it to impersonate people or to create
  deceptive content without consent.

# Maya 2 Native **Open speech. Native voices.** Streaming text-to-speech for **11 Indic languages and English**. **12 languages · 20 voices · Voice cloning · Apache-2.0** [Listen](#listen-in-12-languages) · [Get started](#quickstart) · [Explore voices](#voices) · [Benchmarks](#voicearena-benchmark) · [Evaluation](#evaluation) · [Code](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native)
Maya 2 Native brings streaming speech generation to the languages people use every day. Built by **Maya Research**, it generates **24 kHz speech** in 12 languages, with **20 built-in voices** and **zero-shot voice cloning from 3–10 seconds of reference audio**. A voice can speak across languages: a Hindi reference can become Tamil speech. Use it to give a voice agent its next turn, read a story in a familiar language, or build a multilingual interface you can host yourself. The release includes **open weights and inference code**, with a Python API, an OpenAI-compatible speech endpoint, and WebSocket streaming. Continuous batching and CUDA graphs support concurrent generation. ## Watch Maya in action [Open the video](https://huggingface.co/maya-research/maya2-native/resolve/main/Maya%20Final%20with%20Changes.mp4) · [View on Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1WRd_e8TztpvX1n-DbOBlDj-zP89WE4oX/view) ## VoiceArena benchmark **Ranked #2 for Hindi among real-time TTS models on VoiceArena**, with the category set to **All**. The Telugu sample uses **Nivedita**, also trained on English and Hindi. Both demonstrate cross-lingual synthesis. Assamese is cross-lingual for every built-in voice; see [limitations](#limitations). ## Quickstart Use **Linux, Python 3.10–3.12, and an NVIDIA GPU with a driver supporting CUDA 12.8**. Start with `max_seats=1`. The documented single-seat loading peak is approximately 9.2 GB plus CUDA context; a 12 GB or larger GPU provides more room. See [hardware and memory](#hardware-and-memory) before increasing concurrency. ```bash python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install "maya3[server] @ git+https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native" \ --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 ``` ### Generate speech ```python import soundfile as sf from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) audio = tts.generate( "नमस्ते, आपका ऑर्डर कल पहुँच जाएगा।", lang="hi", voice="Ahana", normalize=True, ) sf.write("speech.wav", audio, 24000) tts.close() ``` `generate()` returns a mono NumPy waveform in `float32`. Model weights, the Mimi codec, and the ECAPA speaker encoder are downloaded on first use. For offline inference, cache all three first, then set `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. **Normalization differs by interface:** the HTTP and WebSocket servers enable it by default. The Python API requires `normalize=True`. It expands numbers, currency, dates, times, URLs, email addresses, and other written forms into spoken text. Check the output for unusual formats.
Stream audio as it is generated ### Stream speech ```python from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) try: with open("speech.pcm", "wb") as output: for chunk in tts.stream( "Your order has shipped and will arrive tomorrow.", lang="en", voice="Siddhant", normalize=True, ): output.write(chunk.astype(" ### Clone a voice across languages Use a clean, single-speaker reference clip and its exact transcript. Obtain the speaker's permission before cloning their voice. The reference language and the output language can differ. ```python import soundfile as sf from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) tts.register_voice( "my_voice", ref_audio="reference.wav", # 3–10 seconds recommended ref_text="", lang="hi", # reference language ) audio = tts.generate( "வணக்கம், எப்படி இருக்கிறீர்கள்?", lang="ta", # output language voice="my_voice", normalize=True, ) sf.write("cloned_voice_tamil.wav", audio, 24000) tts.close() ``` The default cloning mode, `icl_spk`, combines the reference audio with an ECAPA speaker embedding. Clones approximate the reference voice; similarity and accent vary. A dedicated cloning benchmark is not included in this release's reported results.
Run a local HTTP and WebSocket server ### Serve over HTTP or WebSocket ```bash python -m maya3.server \ --ckpt maya-research/maya2-native \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --max-seats 1 ``` After `GET /health` reports ready, generate speech: ```bash curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/audio/speech \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"input":"Your order has shipped.","language":"en","voice":"Ahana","response_format":"wav"}' \ --output speech.wav ``` The server provides `POST /v1/audio/speech`, `WS /v1/tts/stream`, and voice registration endpoints. It has no built-in authentication; add authentication and access controls before exposing it beyond a trusted environment. See the [GitHub README](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native#serve-the-model) for clients and protocol details.

Malayalam · `mr` Marathi · `or` Odia · `pa` Punjabi · `ta` Tamil · `te` Telugu. Pass only the speech text and the voice name to the API. The engine constructs the voice prompt internally; adding `Ahana:` to your text is unnecessary. Use either a built-in voice or your own reference audio for a request, rather than combining them. ## Evaluation The release was evaluated on **6,000 held-out texts across 12 languages**, producing **20.3 hours of speech**. Three ASR judges measured intelligibility; a speaker-embedding classifier measured consistency among the 20 built-in voices. **These are Maya Research's release measurements.** ASR error rates and embedding similarity capture specific aspects of quality; they do not replace human listening or measure every aspect of naturalness. Serving measurements below describe the tested hardware and workload. ### Benchmark design The release benchmark, **bench6k**, contains **6,000 held-out texts: 500 per language across 31 content categories**, including conversation, names, numbers, dates, currency, addresses, URLs, code-mixed text, tongue twisters, and prompts of 1–50 words. The release documentation states that these evaluation texts were excluded from training. The benchmark produced **20.3 hours of speech** through the server, with normalization and engine guards enabled, sampled decoding, and one seed per row. Voices were distributed across languages and categories; long inputs used the serving stack's text chunking. Three ASR systems transcribed the generated speech: - **ASR-1:** Maya's in-house Indic ASR and primary judge. - **Qwen3-ASR:** a third ASR judge. - **ASR-2:** a second in-house Indic ASR, held out from training, reward generation, and checkpoint selection. **Character error rate (CER)** compares ASR transcripts with spoken-form references. Scorer v1 uses the benchmark's normalization and script harmonization. Scorer v2 additionally harmonizes Latin and native-script spellings in code-mixed spans. The two scorers evaluate the same generated audio; lower v2 scores reflect a scoring change. | Overall CER ↓ | ASR-1 | Qwen3-ASR | ASR-2, held out | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Scorer v1 | 3.49% | 3.40% | 2.86% | | Scorer v2, additional code-mix harmonization | 2.35% | 2.22% | 1.73% | ### Results by language CER below uses **scorer v1**. Voice identity is nearest-centroid classification among the 20 built-in voices, using ECAPA embeddings from clips of at least one second. It is a closed-set identity metric, separate from zero-shot clone similarity. | Language | Code | CER ASR-1 ↓ | CER Qwen3-ASR ↓ | CER ASR-2 ↓ | Voice identity ↑ | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Assamese | `as` | 5.41% | 6.59% | 5.54% | 96.4% | | Bengali | `bn` | 2.60% | 2.83% | 2.68% | 98.5% | | English | `en` | 9.69% | 1.74% | 1.43% | 99.6% | | Gujarati | `gu` | 2.25% | 3.76% | 2.26% | 98.9% | | Hindi | `hi` | 1.52% | 2.05% | 1.57% | 99.6% | | Kannada | `kn` | 2.28% | 2.72% | 2.23% | 97.9% | | Malayalam | `ml` | 3.75% | 4.20% | 4.03% | 99.4% | | Marathi | `mr` | 1.66% | 2.09% | 1.54% | 99.1% | | Odia | `or` | 3.45% | 4.33% | 3.54% | 97.4% | | Punjabi | `pa` | 2.51% | 3.32% | 2.66% | 99.1% | | Tamil | `ta` | 4.42% | 4.55% | 4.33% | 98.1% | | Telugu | `te` | 2.29% | 2.64% | 2.53% | 99.4% | ASR-1's English CER is substantially higher than the other two judges. The release analysis attributes part of this difference to ASR-1 looping on spoken URLs such as “W W W.” All three results are retained to show judge disagreement. ### Failures and voice consistency The benchmark's **consensus failure rate** requires agreement between ASR-1 and Qwen3-ASR under the release's failure rules, covering looping, substantial insertions, very high CER, and duration-limit events. | Release measurement | Result | |---|---:| | Consensus failure rate, scorer v1 | 0.15% | | Consensus failure rate, scorer v2 | 0.03% | | Outputs reaching the absolute length cap | 0.00% | | Loops / truncations | 0.02% / 0.13% | | Built-in voice name spoken aloud | 0.00% | | Voice identity, nearest of 20 centroids | 98.6% | | Mean ECAPA similarity | 0.778 | Zero observed events apply to this finite benchmark. A consensus failure rate does not count every pronunciation error or one-judge disagreement. A separate 1,248-row named-voice evaluation reports 98.9% identity in trained languages and 98.8% cross-lingual identity. The same classifier scored 98.0% on held-out recordings of the source voices. These are task-specific measurements, rather than evidence that generated speech is more natural than recorded speech. ### Harder inputs | Category | ASR-1 CER, v1 | ASR-1 CER, v2 | |---|---:|---:| | Web addresses | 29.06% | 20.34% | | Heavy code-mix | 16.74% | 4.11% | | Code-mix | 10.60% | 3.51% | | Symbols | 6.34% | 2.49% | The code-mix gap illustrates the effect of script spelling on ASR-based scoring. Pronunciation and intelligibility still need listening evaluation, especially for names, URLs, and critical numbers. ### Streaming performance The reported release serving run used **one H100 NVL with 95 GB reported memory**, **224 concurrent WebSocket streams**, a BF16 backbone, and an FP16 depth decoder. | Metric | Reported result | |---|---:| | Concurrent streams | 224 | | Aggregate throughput | 323 seconds of audio per wall-clock second | | Time to first audio, steady state, p50 / p90 / p99 | 111 / 134 / 242 ms | | Time to first audio, complete run including ramp and drain, p50 / p99 | 115 / 774 ms | | Per-stream real-time factor at full load, p50 | 0.68 | | Observed playback stalls / serving errors | 0 / 0 | A separate single-stream H100 measurement reports approximately **14 ms to first audio** and **0.13 real-time factor**. It uses a different load condition from the 224-stream run. Real-time factor is generation time divided by audio duration; lower is faster. The release analysis attributes the complete-run latency tail partly to admission queuing during the drain phase. Latency depends on hardware, load, input length, cached state, and the serving environment; these measurements do not establish public internet or telephone latency. ## Hardware and memory The engine documentation reports the following GPU allocator measurements with a BF16 backbone, FP16 depth decoder, and **2,048 KV-cache tokens per seat**. Add approximately **0.5 GB for the CUDA context** and allow additional deployment headroom. | Concurrent seats | Steady GPU memory | Peak during loading | |---|---:|---:| | 1 | 7.7 GB | 9.2 GB | | 8 | 9.7 GB | 10.9 GB | | 16 | 11.7 GB | 12.8 GB | | 32 | 15.8 GB | 16.5 GB | `max_seats` controls allocated serving capacity and memory, even before every seat is busy. These figures describe this configuration; a checkpoint's download size is smaller than its total runtime memory requirement. See [engine documentation](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native/blob/main/docs/ENGINE.md) for configuration and hardware-specific measurements.
Architecture and audio generation ## Architecture Maya 2 Native generates discrete audio tokens autoregressively, then decodes them into speech with Mimi. | Component | Description | |---|---| | Text and audio backbone | Initialized from [Qwen3-1.7B-Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base); 28 layers, hidden size 2,048, 16 attention heads and 8 KV heads; extended vocabulary for language and audio tokens | | Depth decoder | Approximately 555M parameters; predicts codebooks 1–31 after the backbone predicts codebook 0 | | Audio codec | [Kyutai Mimi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/mimi); 32 codebooks with 2,048 entries each, at 12.5 frames per second | | Speaker conditioning | 192-dimensional [SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN](https://huggingface.co/speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb) embedding projected into the backbone; reference-audio conditioning for cloning | | Output | 24 kHz mono speech, 80 ms per audio frame | At each step, the backbone predicts the first codebook, the depth decoder fills the remaining codebooks, and Mimi decodes an audio frame. The engine can emit that frame while generation continues. An end-of-audio token controls normal stopping; duration and loop guards provide additional controls.
## Training data and procedure The release documentation describes a mixture of **licensed and synthetic speech with transcripts** across the 12 languages, plus text-only data used to adapt the backbone to the languages. The built-in voice personas use synthetic and licensed voice data prepared for this purpose. The preference-optimization stage used **direct preference optimization (DPO)** on model-generated candidates ranked by ASR agreement and speaker similarity. Benchmark texts were excluded from training, according to the release documentation. Dataset identities, total training hours, detailed per-language composition, and the full training configuration are not disclosed in this release. Automated scores should be considered alongside these disclosure limits. ## Limitations - **Uneven language coverage.** Assamese is the most challenging Indic language in the release benchmark. No built-in voice has at least one hour of Assamese training data; some outputs drift toward a Bengali-like timbre. Other cross-lingual combinations can also carry the voice's training-language accent. - **Very short turns.** One- or two-word prompts are less stable in voice identity, and speaker-embedding evaluation is less reliable on very short clips. A slightly longer phrase may help short agent responses. - **Code-mixed and written-form inputs.** English words inside Indic sentences vary by voice. URLs, symbols, dates, and long digit sequences remain difficult, even with normalization. Listen to application-specific examples before relying on them. - **Voice cloning.** Similarity is approximate. Noise, multiple speakers, short references, and inaccurate transcripts can degrade results. Dedicated zero-shot cloning scores are not reported here. - **Emotion and events.** Tags such as `[laughs]`, `[sighs]`, `[whispers]`, `[sad]`, and `[excited]` are best effort and were not the focus of this release. - **Generation and guards.** Sampling can produce errors. The same seed is reproducible for an isolated request, but batching changes the random stream. Loop and duration guards can end genuinely repetitive text early. No benchmark clip spoke a built-in voice name aloud, but this remains a possible failure mode. - **Evaluation scope.** Results use automated ASR and speaker-embedding judges. This card does not report a human naturalness study, comprehensive dialect or demographic evaluation, confidence intervals, or a controlled comparison with other TTS models. ## Intended use and responsible deployment Maya 2 Native is intended for voice interfaces and agents, accessibility, reading and narration, IVR, notifications, and research on multilingual speech generation. Clone only voices you own or have explicit permission to use. Disclose synthetic speech to listeners, especially in calls and media. Do not use the model for deceptive impersonation, fraud, harassment, non-consensual content, disinformation, or attempts to defeat voice authentication. Built-in voice names identify synthetic personas and should not be presented as real people. **This release does not add an audio watermark.** Applications should implement the consent, disclosure, access controls, and abuse monitoring appropriate to their use. Consult the repository's [security guidance](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native/blob/main/SECURITY.md) for deployment considerations.
Files in this repository ## Files in this repository | Path | Contents | |---|---| | `model-00001-of-00002.safetensors`, `model-00002-of-00002.safetensors` | BF16 model weight shards | | `model.safetensors.index.json` | Weight-to-shard mapping | | `maya3_config.json` | Resolved model configuration and serialization metadata | | `backbone/` | Backbone configuration and tokenizer; backbone weights are included in the main model shards | | `voices/voices.json` | Built-in voice metadata and conditioning modes | | `samples/` | The twelve WAV examples above | Tied weights are stored once and represented through aliases. Mimi and the ECAPA speaker encoder are resolved from their own repositories on first use.
## License The model weights are released under **Apache-2.0**, as specified in this repository's license metadata. The [inference code](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native) is also Apache-2.0. The upstream components retain their own licenses: **Qwen3-1.7B-Base** (Apache-2.0), **Kyutai Mimi** (CC-BY-4.0), and **SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN** (Apache-2.0). Preserve their notices and attribution when redistributing or using these components. ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{maya2native2026, title = {Maya 2 Native: Streaming Multilingual Text-to-Speech}, author = {{Maya Research}}, year = {2026}, url = {https://huggingface.co/maya-research/maya2-native}, note = {Release 1.0} } ``` ## Credits and acknowledgments **Created by [Maya Research](https://huggingface.co/maya-research).** **Maya Research team** - Dheemanth Reddy BS - Bharath Kumar Kakumani - Sai Charan Thippareddy - Prahalad Boreddy - Nikil Thalapaneni Maya 2 Native builds on the work of the open research community. We thank: - **The Qwen team** for [Qwen3-1.7B-Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base), which initializes the text and audio backbone. - **Kyutai** for [Mimi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/mimi), the neural audio codec used to represent and decode speech. - **The SpeechBrain team** for [ECAPA-TDNN](https://huggingface.co/speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb), used for speaker conditioning and voice-identity evaluation. - **The Hugging Face community** for the tools and infrastructure that make sharing models and building on them easier. --- license: apache-2.0 base_model: ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b base_model_relation: quantized library_name: transcribe.cpp pipeline_tag: automatic-speech-recognition language: - en - fr - de - es - pt - ja tags: - gguf - transcribe.cpp - asr - speech-to-text - granite - granite-speech - audio-llm - multilingual transcribe_cpp: wer_librispeech_test_clean: bf16: 1.31 f16: 1.32 q8_0: 1.32 q6_k: 1.29 q5_k_m: 1.33 q4_k_m: 1.37 rtf_m4_max: metal: 33 cpu: 5.8 rtf_m4: metal: 12 cpu: 4 rtf_ryzen_4750u: vulkan: 2.8 cpu: 1.4 streaming: false translate: true lang_detect: false timestamps: none --- # granite-speech-4.1-2b: transcribe.cpp GGUF GGUF conversions of [ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b) for use with [transcribe.cpp](https://github.com/handy-computer/transcribe.cpp). Ported from upstream commit [8f4bb5f](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b/commit/8f4bb5f), pinned 2026-05-17. Validated against the Transformers reference at transcribe.cpp commit [275332d](https://github.com/handy-computer/transcribe.cpp/tree/275332d) on 2026-05-17. Offline multilingual speech-to-text. IBM Granite Speech 4.1-2b is an audio-LLM with the same architecture as 4.0-1b (Conformer encoder with block-local Shaw attention, BLIP-2 Q-Former projector, Granite-4.0-1b-base autoregressive LLM decoder) and improved punctuation and casing over 4.0-1b. Takes a 16 kHz mono WAV and produces a transcript. Transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese. Translates between English and each of those five other languages in either direction (en ↔ fr, en ↔ de, en ↔ es, en ↔ pt, en ↔ ja) — always via English, no direct fr↔de etc. ## Downloads | Quantization | Download | Size | WER (LibriSpeech test-clean) | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | | BF16 | [granite-speech-4.1-2b-BF16.gguf](https://huggingface.co/handy-computer/granite-speech-4.1-2b-gguf/resolve/main/granite-speech-4.1-2b-BF16.gguf) | 4.63 GB | 1.31% | | F16 | [granite-speech-4.1-2b-F16.gguf](https://huggingface.co/handy-computer/granite-speech-4.1-2b-gguf/resolve/main/granite-speech-4.1-2b-F16.gguf) | 4.63 GB | 1.32% | | Q8_0 | [granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q8_0.gguf](https://huggingface.co/handy-computer/granite-speech-4.1-2b-gguf/resolve/main/granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q8_0.gguf) | 2.56 GB | 1.32% | | Q6_K | [granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q6_K.gguf](https://huggingface.co/handy-computer/granite-speech-4.1-2b-gguf/resolve/main/granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q6_K.gguf) | 2.02 GB | 1.29% | | Q5_K_M | [granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q5_K_M.gguf](https://huggingface.co/handy-computer/granite-speech-4.1-2b-gguf/resolve/main/granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q5_K_M.gguf) | 1.83 GB | 1.33% | | Q4_K_M | [granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q4_K_M.gguf](https://huggingface.co/handy-computer/granite-speech-4.1-2b-gguf/resolve/main/granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q4_K_M.gguf) | 1.60 GB | 1.37% | WER measured on the full LibriSpeech test-clean split (2620 utterances) with greedy decoding. BF16 reference baseline (re-run locally with the model card's exact prompt): 1.31% — 0.02pp below upstream's published 1.33%, likely a minor normalization difference on the publisher side and well within bootstrap CI overlap. Text normalizer: Whisper `EnglishTextNormalizer`, the same normalizer Open ASR Leaderboard uses. ## Usage Build transcribe.cpp from source: ```bash git clone git@github.com:handy-computer/transcribe.cpp.git cd transcribe.cpp cmake -B build && cmake --build build ``` Run on a 16 kHz mono WAV: ```bash build/bin/transcribe-cli \ -m granite-speech-4.1-2b-Q8_0.gguf \ input.wav ``` If your audio isn't already 16 kHz mono WAV, convert it first: ```bash ffmpeg -i input.mp3 -ar 16000 -ac 1 output.wav ``` See the [transcribe.cpp model page](https://github.com/handy-computer/transcribe.cpp/blob/main/docs/models/granite-speech-4.1-2b.md) for performance numbers, numerical validation, and reproduction steps. ## License Inherited from the base model: **Apache-2.0**. See the [upstream model card](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b) for full terms. --- ## Original Model Card > The section below is reproduced from > [ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b) at commit > `8f4bb5f` for offline reference. The upstream card is the > authoritative source. # Granite-Speech-4.1-2B **Model Summary:** Granite Speech 4.1 2B is a compact and efficient speech-language model, specifically designed for multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) and bidirectional automatic speech translation (AST) for English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese and Japanese. The model was trained on 174,000 hours of audio from public corpora for ASR and AST as well as synthetic datasets tailored to support Japanese ASR, keyword-biased ASR and speech translation. Granite Speech 4.1 2B was trained by modality aligning an intermediate checkpoint of [granite-4.0-1b-base](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-1b-base) to speech on publicly available open source corpora containing audio inputs and text targets. Compared to its predecessor [granite-4.0-1b-speech](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-1b-speech), this model has the same parameter count (the new naming convention reflects actual instead of base LLM size) and provides additional capabilities and improvements: * Higher transcription accuracy for multilingual ASR due to a novel dual-head CTC encoder with both graphemic and BPE outputs and frame importance sampling to focus on informative parts of the audio * Punctuation and truecasing for ASR and AST in all languages (including German noun capitalization) with a simple prompt change * Better keyword list biasing capability for enhanced recognition of names, acronyms and technical jargon Two additional model variants explore different capabilities and inference optimization: * [granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus) adds speaker-attributed ASR and word-level time stamps * [granite-speech-4.1-2b-nar](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b-nar) introduces a novel non-autoregressive architecture for higher throughput **Evaluations:** We evaluated granite-speech-4.1-2b alongside other speech-language models in the less than 8b parameter range as well as dedicated ASR and AST systems on standard benchmarks. The evaluation spanned multiple public benchmarks, with particular emphasis on English ASR tasks while also including multilingual ASR and AST for X-En and En-X translations.
![granite-speech-4.1-2b-wer1-crop](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/666ec38102791b3b49f453e8/wY8LOsUVOcb0k204YpdL7.png)
![granite-speech-4.1-2b-wer2-crop](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/666ec38102791b3b49f453e8/5nnbHPrni3qCNjzkHfod0.png)
![granite-speech-4.1-2b-bleu1-crop](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/666ec38102791b3b49f453e8/vSmku2veF23Sn0JWplD3j.png)
![granite-speech-4.1-2b-bleu2-crop](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/666ec38102791b3b49f453e8/AEasS_ygOZpqsDoQVL9BC.png)
Performance on the [Open ASR leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_asr_leaderboard) (as of April 2026): ![rtfx_wer](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/666ec38102791b3b49f453e8/uLLMMTQD8CTpvJtou7do9.png)
We evaluated the model’s keyword list biasing (KWB) capability by comparing performance with and without KWB applied at inference time. We report the F1 scores of transcribed keywords during ASR tasks, excluding common words from the evaluation. ![kwb-f1.v2](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/666ec38102791b3b49f453e8/nNb161Sc_DKC3TONbkbGK.jpeg) We also evaluated our model on a variety of corpora to assess its punctuation and capitalization capabilities. We report the metrics as defined in [LibriSpeech-PC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02943). PER (punctuation error rate) measures errors in the insertion, deletion, or substitution of punctuation marks (periods, commas, and question marks). Cap-F1 (capitalization F1) measures how accurately the model capitalizes relevant words in the output. Note that our Cap-F1 is computed on Levenshtein-aligned matching word pairs rather than fully matching sentences, allowing evaluation even in the presence of ASR errors. | Test Set | PER (↓) | Cap-F1 (↑) | |:---------|:----:|:------:| | LScln | 25.70 | 89.71 | | LSoth | 22.27 | 91.26 | | VoxPopuli | 24.86 | 95.35 | | Earnings-22 | 22.87 | 95.19 | | CV-EN | 9.13 | 96.75 | | CV-DE | 3.66 | 99.50† | | CV-ES | 11.61 | 95.68 | | CV-FR | 11.00 | 97.25 | | CV-PT | 7.86 | 98.51 | † *We report a Cap-F1 of 99.5 on German, where noun capitalization is required.*
**Release Date**: April 29, 2026 **License:** [Apache 2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) **Supported Languages:** English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Japanese **Intended Use:** The model is intended to be used in enterprise applications that involve processing of speech inputs. In particular, the model is well-suited for English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese and Japanese speech-to-text and speech translations to and from English for the same languages, plus English-to-Italian and English-to-Mandarin. ## Usage: Granite Speech model is supported natively in `transformers>=4.52.1`. Below is a simple example of how to use the `granite-speech-4.1-2b` model. ### Usage with `transformers` First, make sure to install a recent version of transformers: ```shell pip install transformers torchaudio soundfile ``` Then run the code: ```python import torch import torchaudio from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from transformers import AutoModelForSpeechSeq2Seq, AutoProcessor device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" model_name = "ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_name) tokenizer = processor.tokenizer model = AutoModelForSpeechSeq2Seq.from_pretrained( model_name, device_map=device, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 ) # Load audio audio_path = hf_hub_download(repo_id=model_name, filename="multilingual_sample.wav") wav, sr = torchaudio.load(audio_path, normalize=True) assert wav.shape[0] == 1 and sr == 16000 # mono, 16kHz # Create text prompt user_prompt = "<|audio|>transcribe the speech with proper punctuation and capitalization." chat = [ {"role": "user", "content": user_prompt}, ] prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(chat, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) # Run the processor + model model_inputs = processor(prompt, wav, device=device, return_tensors="pt").to(device) model_outputs = model.generate( **model_inputs, max_new_tokens=200, do_sample=False, num_beams=1 ) # Transformers includes the input IDs in the response num_input_tokens = model_inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] new_tokens = model_outputs[0, num_input_tokens:].unsqueeze(0) output_text = tokenizer.batch_decode( new_tokens, add_special_tokens=False, skip_special_tokens=True ) print(f"STT output = {output_text[0]}") ``` ### Usage with `vLLM` First, make sure to install vLLM: ```shell pip install vllm ``` * Code for offline mode: ```python from transformers import AutoTokenizer from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams from vllm.assets.audio import AudioAsset model_id = "ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) def get_prompt(question: str, has_audio: bool): """Build the input prompt to send to vLLM.""" if has_audio: question = f"<|audio|>{question}" chat = [ { "role": "user", "content": question } ] return tokenizer.apply_chat_template(chat, tokenize=False) model = LLM( model=model_id, max_model_len=2048, # This may be needed for lower resource devices. limit_mm_per_prompt={"audio": 1}, ) question = "can you transcribe the speech into a written format?" prompt_with_audio = get_prompt( question=question, has_audio=True, ) audio = AudioAsset("mary_had_lamb").audio_and_sample_rate inputs = { "prompt": prompt_with_audio, "multi_modal_data": { "audio": audio, } } outputs = model.generate( inputs, sampling_params=SamplingParams( temperature=0.2, max_tokens=64, ), ) print(f"Audio Example - Question: {question}") print(f"Generated text: {outputs[0].outputs[0].text}") ``` * Code for online mode: ```python """ Launch the vLLM server with the following command: vllm serve ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b \ --api-key token-abc123 \ --max-model-len 2048 """ import base64 import requests from openai import OpenAI from vllm.assets.audio import AudioAsset # Modify OpenAI's API key and API base to use vLLM's API server. openai_api_key = "token-abc123" openai_api_base = "http://localhost:8000/v1" client = OpenAI( # defaults to os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY") api_key=openai_api_key, base_url=openai_api_base, ) model_name = "ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b" # Any format supported by librosa is supported audio_url = AudioAsset("mary_had_lamb").url # Use base64 encoded audio in the payload def encode_audio_base64_from_url(audio_url: str) -> str: """Encode an audio retrieved from a remote url to base64 format.""" with requests.get(audio_url) as response: response.raise_for_status() result = base64.b64encode(response.content).decode("utf-8") return result audio_base64 = encode_audio_base64_from_url(audio_url=audio_url) question = "can you transcribe the speech into a written format?" chat_completion_with_audio = client.chat.completions.create( messages=[{ "role": "user", "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": question }, { "type": "audio_url", "audio_url": { # Any format supported by librosa is supported "url": f"data:audio/ogg;base64,{audio_base64}" }, }, ], }], temperature=0.2, max_tokens=64, model=model_name, ) print(f"Audio Example - Question: {question}") print(f"Generated text: {chat_completion_with_audio.choices[0].message.content}") ``` **Preferred prompt by task:** | Task | Prompt | Notes | |---------|----|------| | ASR (raw transcripts) | ```can you transcribe the speech into a written format?``` | Multilingual prompts supported e.g. ```Pouvez‑vous reconnaître le contenu de la parole ?```| | ASR (with punctuation) | ```transcribe the speech with proper punctuation and capitalization.``` | Non-English ASR requires English prompt | | ASR (with keyword biasing) | ```transcribe the speech to text. Keywords: , , ...``` | Non-English ASR requires English prompt | | AST (raw transcripts) | ```translate the speech to .``` | ``````= English, French, German, Spanish, Japanese, Italian, Mandarin | | AST (with punctuation) | ```translate the speech to with proper punctuation and capitalization.``` | Only English prompt supported | | AST (with keyword biasing) | ```translate the speech to . Keywords: , , ...``` | Only English prompt supported | **Model Architecture:** The architecture of granite-speech-4.1-2b consists of the following components: (1) Speech encoder: 16 conformer blocks trained with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) with two classification heads (characters and BPE units) on the subset containing only ASR corpora (see configuration below). The character vocabulary consists of the first 256 ASCII entries for the European languages plus a 92 phonetic Katakana character set for Japanese whereas the BPE units come from the granite 4.0 tokenizer. In addition, our CTC encoder uses block-attention with 4-seconds audio blocks and self-conditioned CTC from the middle layer. The middle layer also provides non-blank probabilities that are used for frame-level posterior-weighted pooling with a window size of 4 for BPE classification. | Configuration parameter | Value | |-----------------|----------------------| | Input dimension | 160 (80 logmels x 2) | | Nb. of layers | 16 | | Hidden dimension | 1024 | | Nb. of attention heads | 8 | | Attention head size | 128 | | Convolution kernel size | 15 | | Output dimension (characters) | 348 | | Output dimension (BPE) | 100353 | (2) Speech projector and temporal downsampler (speech-text modality adapter): we use a 2-layer window query transformer (q-former) operating on blocks of 15 1024-dimensional acoustic embeddings coming out of the last conformer block of the speech encoder that get downsampled by a factor of 5 using 3 trainable queries per block and per layer. The total temporal downsampling factor is 10 (2x from the encoder and 5x from the projector) resulting in a 10Hz acoustic embeddings rate for the LLM. The projector and LLM LoRA adapters were trained jointly on all the corpora mentioned under **Training Data**. (3) Large language model: intermediate checkpoint of granite-4.0-1b-base with 128k context length (https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-1b-base) finetuned on all the corpora mentioned under **Training Data**. **Training Data:** Overall, our training data is largely comprised of two key sources: (1) publicly available datasets (2) Synthetic data created from publicly available datasets specifically targeting Japanese ASR, keyword list-prompted ASR and the speech translation task. A detailed description of the training datasets can be found in the table below: | Name | Task | Nb. hours | Source | |-----------|--------------|----------------|--------------| | CommonVoice-17 En,De,Es,Fr,Pt,Ja | ASR | 5700 | https://huggingface.co/datasets/mozilla-foundation/common_voice_17_0 | | MLS En,De,Es,Fr,Pt | ASR | 48000 | https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/multilingual_librispeech | | Librispeech English | ASR | 1000 | https://huggingface.co/datasets/openslr/librispeech_asr | | Librispeech-PC English     | ASR | # KittenTTS 2

A 1.7B speech language model with in-context voice cloning. It reads text and writes S3
codec tokens, which a vocoder turns into 24 kHz audio.

```bash
pip install kittenml
```

```python
from kittenml import KittenTTS
import soundfile as sf

m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2")

# a built-in voice
audio = m.generate("Hi! umm.. how are you, I guess?  .. uh.. nice to meet you??",
                   voice="WeatherPresenterCheerful")

# or clone one, from 5-30 seconds of a single speaker
audio = m.generate("This is my own voice.", reference="my_voice.wav")

sf.write("output.wav", audio, m.sample_rate)
```

Everything the model needs is in this repository, so no Hugging Face login is required.

## Voices

`m.available_voices` lists all 115. Bella, Jasper, Luna, Bruno, Rosie, Hugo, Kiki
and Leo are the same speakers as in KittenTTS 0.8, so existing code keeps working.

Voices named after a person are English. The rest are named for the language they
speak followed by what they are — `SpanishAbuela`, `JapaneseTrainConductor`,
`RussianBabushka` — and are how you reach those languages, since the voice is what
carries the accent. Nine older entries carry a bare language name: Arabic, Chinese,
French, German, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish.

```python
m.generate("Guten Morgen. Ich wünsche dir einen wunderschönen Tag.",
           voice="German", normalize=False)

m.generate("Buenas tardes. Hoy vamos a preparar algo muy especial.",
           voice="SpanishAbuela", normalize=False)
```

Sixteen languages have a named voice: Arabic, Chinese, Dutch, French, German, Hindi,
Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Turkish,
and English.

Pass `normalize=False` for non-English text: the text normalizer is English-tuned and
will mangle numbers and dates in other languages.

## Expression controls

> **Beta.** Emotion control steers delivery rather than guaranteeing it, and the effect
> varies by voice and by sentence.

```python
m.generate("[joyful] We won the grant <laugh> I can (((hardly))) believe it!",
           voice="Kiki", preset="expressive")
```

A leading `[emotion]` tag, inline `<event>` tags and `(((emphasis)))` spans reach the
model as markup rather than being spoken, and switch on its expression conditioning.

**Emotions** — one leading tag sets the emotion for the whole line:

`[angry]` `[contemplative]` `[excited]` `[joyful]` `[mundane]`
`[nervous]` `[sad]` `[stern]` `[surprised]` `[tender]`

**Vocal events** — inline, anywhere in the line:

`<gasp>` `<giggle>` `<growl>` `<gulp>` `<laugh>`
`<pause>` `<scoff>` `<sigh>` `<sob>` `<um>`

**Emphasis** — triple parentheses stress a word or short phrase:

```python
m.generate("I told you (((never))) to open that door.", voice="Victor")
```

Only these twenty tags are recognised. They are the most common of the many in the
training data, so a rarer one such as `[reverent]` is spoken as ordinary text rather
than treated as markup — as is anything else bracketed, like `section [3]` or `x < 5`.

## Weight variants

The language model ships in three packings of the same weights. `weights=` picks one;
`model.available_weights` lists them.

| `weights=` | On disk | |
|---|---|---|
| `"packed"` *(default)* | 954 MB | 1.58-bit ternary body, bf16 embedding. **Lossless** |
| `"emb4"` | 469 MB | Same body in TL2, plus a 4-bit embedding. **Lossy** |
| `"full"` | 3469 MB | Plain bf16 |

```python
m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2", weights="emb4")
```

Only the variant you ask for is downloaded.

`emb4` halves the download, and the saving is almost entirely the token embedding — 324M
parameters that `packed` has to leave at bf16 because they are not ternary. Its transformer
body is still bit-exact: all 313 non-embedding tensors reproduce `full` exactly. The
embedding is not, at L2 relative error 0.118 against the bf16 export, and it is coded at
4.21 bits per weight across three frequency tiers. That is the one lossy thing here, which
is why `packed` stays the default.

## Decoders

Audio is decoded in two stages, and the first can be swapped for a smaller distilled
student with weights packed to 4 or 8 bits:

```python
m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2", decoder="student_w4")
```

| Decoder | Flow on disk | |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | 459 MB | Best quality |
| `student_w4` | 39 MB | Distilled single-step student, weights packed to 4 bits |

These trade fidelity for footprint, not for speed: quantisation shrinks storage and
memory bandwidth, not arithmetic.

## What is in here

```
lm/          the speech language model, plus its spk_proj speaker head
speaker/     the speaker-embedding model used when cloning
voices/      reference clips, transcripts, and precomputed embeddings
decoders/    the optional 4-bit decoder
cpp/         GGUF weights for the llama.cpp fork, see "Running on CPU"
config.json  token layout, decode presets, voice and decoder indexes
```

The weights are 947 MiB: 910 MiB for the language model and 37 MiB for the decoder.
A load pulls those rather than the whole repository, and only the decoder you ask for.

The language model's linear weights are ternary — within every 128-wide group each
value is exactly one of `{-scale, 0, +scale}` — so bf16 spends 16 bits to say one of
three things. `lm/model-ternary.safetensors` packs them five trits to a byte, 1.6 bits
per weight, with each group keeping its scale at full precision:

| | |
|---|---|
| `lm/model.safetensors` | 3.47 GB, bf16 throughout |
| `lm/model-ternary.safetensors` | **0.95 GB**, the same weights, 3.6x smaller |

The packing is exact rather than approximate, so the two produce bit-identical audio.
`config.json` points `lm_packed` at the smaller file and that is what gets downloaded;
the full file stays for anything loading this with plain `transformers`.

## Running on CPU

KittenTTS 2 runs on CPU out of the box — `device` is auto-detected — but the fastest way
is [kitten-tts-2-cpp](https://github.com/KittenML/kitten-tts-2-cpp), our llama.cpp fork.
The `cpp/` directory here holds what it needs: the GGUF language model and its decoders.

## Requirements

Python 3.10 or later, and PyTorch.

## License

These weights are released under the [Stellon Labs Community License](LICENSE.md). Research,
non-commercial and limited commercial use are free of charge; the commercial grant ends once you
or your affiliates pass USD $1,000,000 in annual revenue or in total cumulative funding, at which
point you need a separate license from Stellon Labs. Distributing the weights, a derivative, or a
product built on them carries attribution requirements — see Section IV(a).

Two things in here are covered by their own terms instead: `speaker/`, the pyannote
speaker-embedding model, under [MIT](speaker/LICENSE), and the `kittenml` Python package that
loads this repository, under Apache 2.0.
